<section class="chapter" id="foundations">
  <div class="wrap">
    <header class="chapter-head rv">
      <span class="kicker">Module 01 — Foundations</span>
      <h2>Every model is a <em>function</em> waiting to be shaped.</h2>
      <p class="lede">Machine learning reframes a problem: instead of writing the rules, you write a <strong>parameterized function</strong> and let data determine its parameters. Everything else in this course — architectures, data pipelines, metrics — exists in service of that one act: fitting <code>f(x)</code> so that <code>f(x)</code> ≈ <code>y</code>.</p>
    </header>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">1.1</span>What a model actually is</h3>
      <p>A model is a family of functions. A linear model is <code>ŷ = w·x + b</code> — the <em>family</em> is all lines, and the <em>parameters</em> (<code>w</code>, <code>b</code>) pick one specific line. A neural network is the same idea taken to the extreme: a function whose shape is so flexible that it can approximate essentially any mapping given enough width and depth. Training is the process of navigating parameter space until the function behaves the way you want.</p>
      <div class="pipe rv" style="--d:.1s">
        <div class="pipe-step"><b>STEP 1</b><span>Collect</span><small>Raw signals — logs, images, text, sensors.</small></div>
        <div class="pipe-step"><b>STEP 2</b><span>Structure</span><small>Clean, label, split into train / val / test.</small></div>
        <div class="pipe-step"><b>STEP 3</b><span>Choose</span><small>Pick an architecture suited to the data.</small></div>
        <div class="pipe-step"><b>STEP 4</b><span>Fit</span><small>Optimize parameters against a loss function.</small></div>
        <div class="pipe-step"><b>STEP 5</b><span>Evaluate</span><small>Measure on held-out data. Iterate honestly.</small></div>
        <div class="pipe-step"><b>STEP 6</b><span>Ship</span><small>Deploy, monitor, and retrain as the world shifts.</small></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">1.2</span>The three learning paradigms</h3>
      <div class="grid c3">
        <div class="card" data-glyph="SUPERVISED"><span class="ctag">Labeled pairs (x, y)</span><h4>Supervised</h4><p>Learn a mapping from examples. The model is graded on every prediction. The workhorse of classification and regression — and the setting where most of this course lives.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="UNSUPERVISED"><span class="ctag">Unlabeled structure</span><h4>Unsupervised</h4><p>Find structure with no labels: clusters, latent factors, compressed representations. Clustering, dimensionality reduction, and — crucially — the self-supervised pretraining that powers modern AI.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="REINFORCEMENT"><span class="ctag">Reward signals</span><h4>Reinforcement</h4><p>An agent learns policies by trial, error, and delayed reward. Slower and noisier to train, but the path to behavior: robotics, game play, and RLHF alignment for language models.</p></div>
      </div>
      <div class="callout key rv"><span class="ct">In practice</span><p>State-of-the-art systems rarely pick just one. A typical LLM is <strong>self-supervised</strong> (predict next token) for most of its compute, then <strong>supervised fine-tuned</strong> on demonstrations, then <strong>reinforcement-tuned</strong> against preferences. Paradigms stack; the fundamentals don't change.</p></div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">1.3</span>Loss, gradients, and the engine of learning</h3>
      <p>Training needs three ingredients: a <strong>loss function</strong> that scores how wrong the model is, a <strong>differentiable path</strong> from parameters to that score, and an <strong>optimizer</strong> that walks the parameters downhill. The magic ingredient is the <em>chain rule</em> — backpropagation — which computes the gradient of the loss with respect to <em>every</em> parameter in a single backward pass.</p>
<pre><span class="cm"># the entire training loop, honestly compressed</span>
<span class="kw">for</span> batch <span class="kw">in</span> dataloader:
    x, y = batch
    y_hat = model(x)              <span class="cm"># forward pass</span>
    loss  = criterion(y_hat, y)   <span class="cm"># how wrong?</span>
    loss.backward()               <span class="cm"># backprop: ∂loss/∂θ</span>
    optimizer.step()              <span class="cm"># nudge parameters</span>
    optimizer.zero_grad()</pre>
      <p>Autograd frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow) build a computation graph during the forward pass and apply the chain rule automatically. Your job is to design the graph; the framework does the calculus.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="exercise rv">
      <span class="etag">Exercise 01</span>
      <ol>
        <li>Take the iris dataset and fit <code>sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression</code>.</li>
        <li>Print <code>coef_</code> and <code>intercept_</code> — these <em>are</em> the learned function. Which feature dominates for each class?</li>
        <li>Now fit the same model on 30 samples. Compare the coefficients. What does that instability teach you about data scale?</li>
      </ol>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">1.4</span>Choosing the right tool</h3>
      <div class="tbl-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>Task shape</th><th>Start here</th><th>Reach for</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td><b>Structured table, clean columns</b></td><td>Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM)</td><td>Logistic / linear regression, small MLPs</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Images, video, raw pixels</b></td><td>Convolutional networks</td><td>ViT-style transformers, diffusion models</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Text and language</b></td><td>Pretrained transformer</td><td>Fine-tune an LLM; fine-tune a smaller one first</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Sequences with local patterns</b></td><td>RNN / GRU / small CNN</td><td>Transformer encoder (attention wins at scale)</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Decisions over time</b></td><td>Value methods, policy gradients</td><td>PPO with a learned reward model</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ======================= MODULE 02 · ARCHITECTURES ======================= -->
<section class="chapter" id="architectures">
  <div class="wrap">
    <header class="chapter-head rv">
      <span class="kicker">Module 02 — Architectures</span>
      <h2>The anatomy of a model: <em>classifiers to transformers</em>.</h2>
      <p class="lede">An architecture is a bet about <strong>structure</strong>. Each family assumes something about how the data is organized — locality in images, order in text, hierarchy in decisions — and encodes that assumption in its wiring. Choosing the right one is 80% of the model design problem.</p>
    </header>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">2.1</span>Linear models & the perceptron</h3>
      <p>The <strong>perceptron</strong> is the atom of deep learning: a dot product plus a threshold. Stack them and you have a network; keep them linear and you have regression. Linear models remain a first resort because they are <em>interpretable</em> — each weight is a direct statement about a feature — and they anchor the intuition: every nonlinearity you add later is a controlled departure from this simple case.</p>
      <div class="grid c2">
        <div class="card" data-glyph="STRENGTHS"><h4>Why they endure</h4><p>Fast to fit, cheap to serve, no hyperparameter maze, and coefficients read like a report. Logistic regression is still the baseline that deep models must beat to earn their GPU time.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="LIMITS"><h4>Where they break</h4><p>A straight line (or hyperplane) cannot carve XOR-shaped decision boundaries. Nonlinear feature engineering becomes unmanageable — which is exactly the gap nonlinear models exist to fill.</p></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">2.2</span>Feedforward networks (MLPs)</h3>
      <p>A multilayer perceptron chains three operations: <strong>affine transform</strong> (learned weights + bias), <strong>nonlinearity</strong> (ReLU, GELU, sigmoid), and <strong>normalization</strong> (BatchNorm / LayerNorm). The universal approximation theorem says one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function — in practice you need <em>many</em> layers, which is why the field went deep.</p>
      <div class="stack rv">
        <div class="layer"><span class="lname">Input</span><span class="ldesc">Raw feature vector <code>x ∈ ℝⁿ</code> — flattened, scaled, ready.</span></div>
        <div class="stack-arrow">↓</div>
        <div class="layer"><span class="lname">Linear</span><span class="ldesc"><code>z = Wx + b</code> — a learned projection into a new geometry.</span></div>
        <div class="stack-arrow">↓</div>
        <div class="layer"><span class="lname">Nonlinear</span><span class="ldesc"><code>σ(z)</code> — ReLU or GELU; without it, depth is just one big matrix.</span></div>
        <div class="stack-arrow">↓</div>
        <div class="layer"><span class="lname">Normalize</span><span class="ldesc">BatchNorm / LayerNorm — keeps activations in a trainable range.</span></div>
        <div class="stack-arrow">↓ × N blocks</div>
        <div class="layer"><span class="lname">Head</span><span class="ldesc">Task output — class logits, a scalar, or a probability vector.</span></div>
      </div>
      <div class="callout rv"><span class="ct">Key idea — expressivity vs. learnability</span><p>More layers and width buy expressivity, but only the <em>right</em> initialization, normalization, and optimizer make that capacity learnable. Architecture is a contract between capacity and optimization.</p></div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">2.3</span>CNNs — vision's local experts</h3>
      <p>Convolutional networks encode a powerful prior: <strong>locality and translation invariance</strong>. Kernels slide across the input, reusing the same weights, building edge → texture → part → object hierarchies while pooling layers shrink spatial dimensions and enlarge receptive fields.</p>
      <div class="tbl-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>Component</th><th>What it does</th><th>Why it matters</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td><b>Conv layer</b></td><td>Sliding kernel extracts local features</td><td>Weight sharing = 100× fewer parameters than a dense layer on images</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Pooling</b></td><td>Downsamples (max / avg / strided conv)</td><td>Grows receptive field, adds robustness to small shifts</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>BatchNorm</b></td><td>Normalizes activations per mini-batch</td><td>Stabilizes training, allows higher learning rates</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Residual skip</b></td><td><code>y = F(x) + x</code> (ResNet)</td><td>Gradients flow unimpeded → networks with 100+ layers</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Global avg pool</b></td><td>Collapses spatial dims to a vector</td><td>Bridges the visual stack to a classification head</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <div class="callout key rv"><span class="ct">Lineage worth knowing</span><p>LeNet (1998) → AlexNet (2012) → VGG / GoogLeNet / ResNet (2014–15) → EfficientNet (2019). Each step was less about a new idea and more about training a bigger one <em>reliably</em>: better initialization, normalization, and skip connections did as much as any structural novelty.</p></div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">2.4</span>RNNs — memory as state</h3>
      <p>Recurrent networks process sequences step by step, carrying a hidden state <code>hₜ = tanh(W·hₜ₋₁ + U·xₜ)</code>. Elegant, but the same matrix is multiplied <em>t</em> times — gradients shrink or explode along the path. <strong>LSTMs</strong> added a gated cell state that can hold information across long spans; <strong>GRUs</strong> simplified the gate structure. For short, tightly local sequences they remain light and effective; for long-range dependencies, attention won.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">2.5</span>Attention & Transformers</h3>
      <p>The transformer replaced recurrence with <strong>attention</strong>: every position can read every other position directly, in parallel. The mechanism is three learned projections — Query, Key, Value — compared pairwise:</p>
<pre><span class="cm"># multi-head attention in four lines</span>
Q, K, V = Wq x, Wk x, Wv x              <span class="cm"># projections</span>
scores  = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k)           <span class="cm"># similarity matrix</span>
attn    = softmax(scores, dim=-1)       <span class="cm"># weight the values</span>
out     = attn @ V                      <span class="cm"># weighted combination</span></pre>
      <div class="tf-fig rv">
        <div class="tf-row">
          <div class="tf-box"><b>Input</b>tokens + positional encoding</div>
          <span class="tf-arrow">→</span>
          <div class="tf-box"><b>Self-Attention</b>every token reads all tokens</div>
          <span class="tf-arrow">→</span>
          <div class="tf-box alt"><b>FFN</b>2-layer MLP per position</div>
          <span class="tf-arrow">→</span>
          <div class="tf-box"><b>Residual + LayerNorm</b>stable gradients</div>
          <span class="tf-arrow">→</span>
          <div class="tf-box alt"><b>× N layers</b>then the task head</div>
        </div>
        <p class="tf-cap">The encoder block. Stack <code>N</code> of them, scale <code>d</code>, and you get the same machine that powers modern language, vision, and multimodal models — the architecture has been stable since 2017; the <em>scale and data</em> are what changed.</p>
      </div>
      <ul class="dash">
        <li><strong>Encoder-only</strong> (BERT-style): bidirectional context → understanding tasks, embeddings, classification.</li>
        <li><strong>Decoder-only</strong> (GPT-style): causal mask, next-token prediction → the dominant architecture for generative LLMs.</li>
        <li><strong>Encoder–decoder</strong> (T5 / original): read with an encoder, generate with a decoder → translation and summarization.</li>
      </ul>
      <div class="callout rv"><span class="ct">Why attention scaled</span><p>Recurrence forces a serial chain of length <code>t</code>; attention computes all pairwise relations at once and parallelizes perfectly on GPUs. The cost is <code>O(t²)</code> memory — which is why modern work keeps reinventing efficient attention (sliding windows, sparsity, linear approximations) rather than abandoning it.</p></div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">2.6</span>Generative models</h3>
      <div class="grid c2">
        <div class="card" data-glyph="GAN"><h4>GANs</h4><p>A generator and discriminator play a min-max game until the generated distribution becomes indistinguishable from real data. Powerful but notoriously unstable to train — mode collapse is the classic failure.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="VAE"><h4>VAEs</h4><p>Learn a smooth probabilistic latent space by matching an encoder's output to a Gaussian prior. Weaker samples, but the most principled latent geometry — and a natural way to regularize any model.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="DIFFUSION"><h4>Diffusion</h4><p>Gradually noisify data to pure noise, then train a network to reverse the process. Iterate the reversal and you sample from the data distribution. The current king of high-fidelity image synthesis.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="AUTOREGRESSIVE"><h4>Autoregressive</h4><p>Model <code>P(x) = Π P(xᵢ | x<ᵢ)</code>: predict the next element, append it, repeat. Simple, flexible, and — via the transformer decoder — the engine of modern text and multimodal generation.</p></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">2.7</span>Ensembles & tree methods</h3>
      <p>Not everything is a neural net. <strong>Random forests</strong> average many decorrelated trees (bagging); <strong>gradient boosting</strong> (XGBoost, LightGBM) sequences trees, each correcting its predecessor's residuals. On tabular data they remain a formidable baseline — often beating neural networks with a fraction of the engineering. A trained model that an ensemble can't improve is a model you can trust.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">2.8</span>Choosing an architecture — a decision rubric</h3>
      <div class="tbl-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>Question</th><th>If…</th><th>Then lean toward</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td><b>What modality?</b></td><td>Images / video</td><td>CNN, ViT, diffusion</td></tr>
            <tr><td></td><td>Text / language</td><td>Transformer (decoder-only for generation)</td></tr>
            <tr><td></td><td>Tabular data</td><td>Boosted trees first, MLP second</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>How much data?</b></td><td>Under ~10⁴ labeled rows</td><td>Simple models + strong features; deep nets overfit</td></tr>
            <tr><td></td><td>10⁶+ samples or tokens</td><td>Deep networks and pretraining pay off</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Latency budget?</b></td><td>Millisecond, edge device</td><td>Small CNN / distilled model / trees</td></tr>
            <tr><td></td><td>Server-side, batched</td><td>Big transformers are affordable</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Interpretability?</b></td><td>Required for compliance</td><td>Linear / trees; probe-based explanations for nets</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="exercise rv">
      <span class="etag">Exercise 02</span>
      <ol>
        <li>Train a 2-layer MLP and a 6-layer MLP (with residual connections) on MNIST. Plot train and validation loss for both.</li>
        <li>Remove the nonlinearity from the 6-layer net. Watch what happens — and explain <em>why</em> in one sentence.</li>
        <li>Now swap ReLU for a constant (identity) with no residual. Compare gradient norms across layers. What did the skip connection do?</li>
      </ol>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ======================= MODULE 03 · DATA ======================= -->
<section class="chapter" id="data">
  <div class="wrap">
    <header class="chapter-head rv">
      <span class="kicker">Module 03 — Data</span>
      <h2>Data preparation is the <em>real</em> model.</h2>
      <p class="lede">There is a quiet law of the field: <strong>models commoditize, data doesn't.</strong> Two teams with identical architectures and compute can land miles apart in accuracy — the difference is almost always upstream of the loss function. This module is where most of your calendar will go.</p>
    </header>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">3.1</span>The seven-stage pipeline</h3>
      <div class="recipe">
        <ol class="steps-ol">
          <li><b>Collection & sourcing</b><span>Define the target population precisely. Data collected outside that population is confidently wrong. Document provenance — you will need it for audits.</span></li>
          <li><b>Cleaning & deduplication</b><span>Fix malformed records, collapse duplicates (exact and near), reconcile units and timezones. Duplicates are silent label-leakage factories.</span></li>
          <li><b>Labeling</b><span>The most expensive stage. Write a labeling rubric <em>before</em> hiring labelers, compute inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ / Krippendorff's α), and route disagreements to adjudication. Your label noise sets the ceiling on achievable accuracy — no model escapes it.</span></li>
          <li><b>Feature engineering</b><span>Encoding (one-hot, target, embeddings), scaling, aggregations, windowed statistics for sequences. For text: tokenization and vocabulary design. For images: resizing, crops, color space.</span></li>
          <li><b>Splitting</b><span>Hold out validation and test sets <em>before</em> any modeling decision. For temporal data: split by time, never randomly. For grouped data: split by group, or you leak.</span></li>
          <li><b>Balancing & weighting</b><span>Address class imbalance with stratification, resampling, or loss weighting — and decide whether the model should optimize accuracy or cost (Module 04 explains why these differ).</span></li>
          <li><b>Packaging & versioning</b><span>Ship datasets as versioned artifacts (DVC, LakeFS, HF Datasets) with a schema, a hash, and a changelog. Reproducibility is a data problem before it is a code problem.</span></li>
        </ol>
        <div class="splitfig rv" style="--d:.15s">
          <h5>Where a dataset's time actually goes</h5>
          <div class="bar-row"><span class="bl">Labeling</span><span class="bar-track"><span class="bar-fill a" style="--w:44%"></span></span><span class="bv">44%</span></div>
          <div class="bar-row"><span class="bl">Cleaning</span><span class="bar-track"><span class="bar-fill a" style="--w:21%"></span></span><span class="bv">21%</span></div>
          <div class="bar-row"><span class="bl">QA / audit</span><span class="bar-track"><span class="bar-fill b" style="--w:14%"></span></span><span class="bv">14%</span></div>
          <div class="bar-row"><span class="bl">Splitting</span><span class="bar-track"><span class="bar-fill b" style="--w:9%"></span></span><span class="bv">9%</span></div>
          <div class="bar-row"><span class="bl">Packaging</span><span class="bar-track"><span class="bar-fill b" style="--w:7%"></span></span><span class="bv">7%</span></div>
          <div class="bar-row"><span class="bl">Sourcing</span><span class="bar-track"><span class="bar-fill b" style="--w:5%"></span></span><span class="bv">5%</span></div>
          <p style="font-size:.82rem;color:var(--ink-mute);margin:14px 0 0">Typical industrial breakdown by engineer-hours. Training itself is rarely the bottleneck.</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">3.2</span>The preprocessing patterns that repeat everywhere</h3>
      <div class="tbl-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>Problem</th><th>Standard treatment</th><th>Classic failure</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td><b>Missing values</b></td><td>Impute (median / model-based) or explicit missing-indicator features</td><td>Imputing on the full set <em>before</em> splitting leaks test information into train</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Scale mismatch</b></td><td>Standardize / min-max <em>fit on train only</em>, apply to val/test</td><td>Scaling on all data — a subtle, pervasive leak</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>High-cardinality categoricals</b></td><td>Target encoding (with smoothing / CV) or learned embeddings</td><td>Naive target encoding overfits; one-hot explodes dimensionality</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Class imbalance</b></td><td>Stratified splits, class weights, focal loss, targeted resampling</td><td>Random resampling duplicates patterns and inflates confidence</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Temporal data</b></td><td>Time-ordered splits, embargo gaps, walk-forward validation</td><td>Random splits that let the model peek at "future" rows</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Text</b></td><span>Tokenization, vocabulary / BPE, truncation or windowing</td><td>Training and inference using different tokenizers</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Images</b></td><td>Resize + random crops/flips (train), center crop (test); augmentation</td><td>Applying test-time transforms only at train time</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <div class="callout key rv"><span class="ct">The cardinal rule</span><p>Every statistic you compute — means, frequencies, encodings, scaler parameters — must be derived from <strong>training data only</strong>, then applied to validation and test. Fit on the fold, transform everything. Frameworks like scikit-learn's <code>Pipeline</code> and <code>cross_val_score</code> exist to make this hard to get wrong. Use them.</p></div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">3.3</span>Data quality: the audits that save you</h3>
      <ul class="dash">
        <li><strong>Distribution drift check</strong> — compare feature distributions across time slices; a silent shift in production is the most common cause of "the model degraded overnight."</li>
        <li><strong>Label audit</strong> — sample 200 labeled examples, re-label blind, and measure agreement. Below κ ≈ 0.6, fix the rubric, not the model.</li>
        <li><strong>Nearest-neighbor dedup</strong> — embedding-based kNN over the corpus to surface near-duplicates across train/val/test boundaries.</li>
        <li><strong>Outlier profiling</strong> — Isolation Forest or per-feature z-score review; decide per feature whether to clip, keep, or drop.</li>
        <li><strong>Representation check</strong> — train a small probe on the frozen features; if the probe can't separate the classes, the features (or labels) are broken.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">3.4</span>The ethics layer</h3>
      <p>Preparation is also where bias is <em>introduced or prevented</em>. Four questions before a dataset ships:</p>
      <ul class="dash">
        <li><strong>Who is missing?</strong> Coverage across demographics, regions, and languages — absence in data is absence in service.</li>
        <li><strong>Whose labels?</strong> Labeler demographics and rubric framing shape what the model considers "normal."</li>
        <li><strong>Consent & rights</strong> — is the source licensed, is PII redacted, does the data contain biometric or health information with special legal status?</li>
        <li><strong>Harm surface</strong> — who bears the cost when this model is wrong, and is that cost symmetric across groups? Run a group-wise fairness slice (Module 04) before launch.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="exercise rv">
      <span class="etag">Exercise 03</span>
      <ol>
        <li>Take any tabular dataset with >5% missingness. Fit a scaler on the <em>full</em> dataset, then fit it on train only. Compare test RMSE between the two pipelines.</li>
        <li>Deliberately create a temporal leak: shuffle a time-series dataset and split randomly. Watch validation performance look "too good."</li>
        <li>Fix it with a time-ordered split and an 11-day embargo. Quantify how much of the "performance" was leakage.</li>
      </ol>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ======================= MODULE 04 · METRICS ======================= -->
<section class="chapter" id="metrics">
  <div class="wrap">
    <header class="chapter-head rv">
      <span class="kicker">Module 04 — Metrics</span>
      <h2>What you measure is what you <em>get</em>.</h2>
      <p class="lede">A metric is a contract between the model and the business. Pick the wrong one and the optimizer will find the most efficient way to fail your actual goal. Precision, recall, F1, AUC, RMSE, BLEU, perplexity — each encodes a different theory of what "good" means. Choose with your eyes open.</p>
    </header>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">4.1</span>Classification, dissected</h3>
      <p>Every classification evaluation starts from the <strong>confusion matrix</strong>. For a binary model on <code>N</code> samples: <code>TP</code> true positives, <code>FP</code> false positives, <code>TN</code> true negatives, <code>FN</code> false negatives. From those four cells:</p>
<pre>accuracy = (TP + TN) / N        <span class="cm"># overall correctness — useless when classes are rare</span>
precision =  TP / (TP + FP)     <span class="cm"># of what you flagged, how much was real?   (cost of false alarms)</span>
recall     =  TP / (TP + FN)    <span class="cm"># of what was real, how much did you catch? (cost of misses)</span>
F1         =  2·P·R / (P + R)   <span class="cm"># harmonic mean — punishes lopsidedness</span>
</pre>
      <p>On an imbalanced dataset (fraud: 0.2% positive), a model that flags <em>nothing</em> scores 99.8% accuracy and catches nothing. <strong>Recall and precision are the honest currencies</strong>; F1 and Fβ (which weights recall vs. precision) let you encode the trade-off numerically — F2 says "missing cases hurt twice as much as false alarms."</p>
      <div class="tbl-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>Scenario</th><th>Priority</th><th>Lead metric</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td><b>Fraud / spam detection</b></td><td>Don't miss real fraud; false alarms tolerable</td><td>Recall @ fixed precision, PR-AUC</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Medical screening</b></td><td>Missing disease is catastrophic</td><td>Sensitivity (recall) at high specificity</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Ad click prediction</b></td><td>Flagging must be trustworthy</td><td>Precision, top-k lift</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Balanced multiclass</b></td><td>Even performance across classes</td><td>Macro-averaged F1</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Rare-class multiclass</b></td><td>Don't let the majority drown the minority</td><td>Weighted F1 / per-class recall report</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">4.2</span>Ranking: ROC and PR curves</h3>
      <p>Real classifiers emit <em>probabilities</em>, and a threshold is a business decision — so evaluate the whole curve, not one cut point. <strong>ROC-AUC</strong> plots TPR vs. FPR across all thresholds and measures the probability that a random positive ranks above a random negative. It looks flattering under extreme imbalance because the FPR denominator is huge. <strong>PR-AUC</strong> plots precision vs. recall and is the correct lens when positives are rare — it answers "when I flag <em>this many</em>, how many are real?"</p>
      <div class="grid c2">
        <div class="card" data-glyph="ROC-AUC"><h4>Use when…</h4><p>Classes are reasonably balanced and you need a threshold-free, threshold-invariant summary. AUC = 0.5 is a coin; 0.9+ is strong; report the confidence interval, not just the point.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="PR-AUC"><h4>Use when…</h4><p>Positives are rare (under ~5%) or the cost asymmetry is extreme. A model can post great ROC-AUC and still be practically useless at the operating point you actually deploy at.</p></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">4.3</span>Regression metrics</h3>
      <div class="tbl-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>Metric</th><th>Formula / idea</th><th>Best for</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td><b>MSE</b></td><td><code>mean((y−ŷ)²)</code></td><td>Default differentiable loss; punishes large errors hard</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>RMSE</b></td><td><code>√MSE</code></td><td>Reporting in target units; same penalty profile as MSE</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>MAE</b></td><td><code>mean(|y−ŷ|)</code></td><td>Robustness to outliers; straight-line interpretation</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Huber</b></td><td>MSE near zero, MAE in the tails</td><td>Noisy labels — get MSE's gradient, MAE's robustness</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Quantile loss</b></td><td>Asymmetric penalty per quantile τ</td><td>Prediction intervals, "95th percentile of delivery time"</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
      <p>Always pair a point metric with an <em>error distribution</em>: mean error (bias), a histogram of residuals, and a Q–Q plot. A model with zero mean error can still be systematically wrong in the tails where the money is.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">4.4</span>Language & generation metrics</h3>
      <ul class="dash">
        <li><strong>Perplexity</strong> — <code>exp(−log-likelihood)</code>; the model's effective branching factor. Excellent for tracking pretraining health; weak as a proxy for task quality.</li>
        <li><strong>BLEU / ROUGE</strong> — n-gram overlap with references. Fast and cheap, but reward fluent <em>generic</em> text over correct specific text. Use for regression monitoring, not go/no-go.</li>
        <li><strong>BERTScore</strong> — embedding similarity between generated and reference tokens. More tolerant of paraphrase; still reference-bound.</li>
        <li><strong>LLM-as-judge</strong> — a strong model grades outputs against a rubric. The current standard for open-ended quality, with real caveats: self-preference bias, positional bias, and rubric drift. Calibrate against human scores on a held-out set.</li>
        <li><strong>Task metrics</strong> — for grounded tasks (code, math, extraction), prefer execution pass rate, exact set match, or schema validation. Verifiable beats vibes.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">4.5</span>Fairness & calibration slices</h3>
      <p>A global metric can hide a failing subgroup. Report your lead metric <em>per slice</em> — by demographic group, region, device, or traffic source — and set launch gates on the worst slice, not the mean. Complement this with <strong>calibration</strong>: if the model says 80%, do 80% of those cases actually occur? A reliability diagram (predicted probability vs. observed frequency) exposes overconfidence; temperature scaling and isotonic regression fix it post-hoc at near-zero cost.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv" id="gaugeBlock">
      <h3><span class="hn">4.6</span>Interactive — feel the precision/recall trade-off</h3>
      <p>Imagine a fraud detector with <strong>900 true frauds and 99,100 legitimate transactions</strong> (0.9% positive rate). Drag the threshold. Watch what "better" actually means when the classes are lopsided.</p>
      <div class="gauge-card rv">
        <svg class="gauge-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" role="img" aria-label="Gauge showing recall and precision for the current threshold">
          <path class="gauge-track" d="M 30 160 A 130 130 0 0 1 290 160"></path>
          <path class="gauge-fill" id="gRecall" d="M 30 160 A 130 130 0 0 1 290 160"></path>
          <text class="gauge-label" x="160" y="118" text-anchor="middle">Recall</text>
          <text class="gauge-center" id="gRecallVal" x="160" y="146" text-anchor="middle">69.1%</text>
          <text class="gauge-label" id="gPrecLabel" x="160" y="182" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--accent-2)">Precision 3.8%</text>
        </svg>
        <div class="gauge-controls">
          <div>
            <label>Decision threshold <output id="gThOut">0.50</output></label>
            <input type="range" id="gTh" min="0.01" max="0.99" step="0.01" value="0.50" aria-label="Decision threshold">
          </div>
          <div class="grid c3" style="gap:10px">
            <div class="card" style="padding:14px"><span class="ctag" style="margin-bottom:4px">TP</span><p style="margin:0;font-family:var(--font-mono);font-size:1.15rem" id="gTP">622</p></div>
            <div class="card" style="padding:14px"><span class="ctag" style="margin-bottom:4px;color:var(--bad)">FP</span><p style="margin:0;font-family:var(--font-mono);font-size:1.15rem" id="gFP">15,723</p></div>
            <div class="card" style="padding:14px"><span class="ctag" style="margin-bottom:4px;color:var(--accent-2)">F1</span><p style="margin:0;font-family:var(--font-mono);font-size:1.15rem" id="gF1">0.072</p></div>
          </div>
        </div>
        <p class="metric-note" id="gNote">At threshold 0.50 the model flags 15,723 clean transactions to catch 622 frauds. In this world, <b>recall is the hero; precision is the bill.</b></p>

      <span class="etag">Exercise 04</span>

<!-- ======================= MODULE 05 · TRAINING ======================= -->
<section class="chapter" id="training">
  <div class="wrap">
    <header class="chapter-head rv">
      <span class="kicker">Module 05 — Training</span>
      <h2>Optimization: walking a <em>mountain range</em> in the dark.</h2>
      <p class="lede">The loss surface of a modern network is non-convex, wildly scaled, and studded with saddle points. Training is the art of still finding a good valley — via the right optimizer, the right schedule, the right regularization, and a healthy skepticism about your own validation curve.</p>
    </header>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">5.1</span>Gradient descent and its descendants</h3>
      <p><strong>Batch GD</strong> computes the exact gradient per step — accurate, but memory-heavy. <strong>SGD</strong> uses one sample — noisy, but the noise is a feature: it escapes sharp minima. <strong>Mini-batch SGD</strong> is the practical middle. Modern optimizers stack clever state on top of SGD:</p>
      <div class="tbl-wrap">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>Optimizer</th><th>Idea</th><th>When to reach for it</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td><b>Momentum</b></td><td>Accumulates a velocity term; smooths oscillations</td><td>Default upgrade over vanilla SGD for deep nets</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>AdaGrad</b></td><td>Per-parameter adaptive LR from accumulated gradients</td><td>Sparse features (early NLP); LR decays too aggressively for dense nets</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>RMSProp</b></td><td>Exponentially-decayed adaptive LR</td><td>Fixes AdaGrad's decay; classic for RNNs</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>Adam</b></td><td>Momentum + RMSProp (1st & 2nd moment estimates)</td><td>The workhorse default; fast, forgiving hyperparameters</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>AdamW</b></td><td>Adam with <em>decoupled</em> weight decay</td><td>Transformers and large-scale training; the modern default</td></tr>
            <tr><td><b>SGD + momentum</b></td><td>The classic, tuned carefully</td><td>Often edges out Adam on final accuracy for CV tasks if you have the tuning budget</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">5.2</span>Learning rate: the number that matters most</h3>
      <p>No hyperparameter changes outcomes as much as the learning rate. Too high and the loss diverges (or oscillates forever); too low and you crawl. The modern playbook:</p>
      <ul class="dash">
        <li><strong>LR range test</strong> — sweep log-spaced LRs for a few hundred steps; pick the highest rate whose loss is still descending (the "no-divergence point," often a hair below the minimum observed loss).</li>
        <li><strong>Warmup</strong> — start small (e.g., 1–5% of peak) and ramp linearly; stabilizes early training when LayerNorm statistics and adapters are still chaotic.</li>
        <li><strong>Scheduled decay</strong> — cosine annealing to a low floor is the transformer standard; step decay remains common in CV.</li>
        <li><strong>Batch-size coupling</b> — larger batches permit higher LRs (linear scaling rule), but reduce the beneficial noise; watch generalization.</li>
        <li><strong>Gradient clipping</b> — clip global norm (typically to 1.0); cheap insurance against explosion, especially in RNNs and early transformer layers.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">5.3</span>Regularization: the anti-overfit toolkit</h3>
      <div class="train-grid">
        <div class="card" data-glyph="DATA"><h4>Augmentation</h4><p>The strongest regularizer in vision: crops, flips, color jitter, MixUp, cutmix. For text: synonym dropout, back-translation. For tabular: controlled noise, feature masking. If your validation gap is your problem, augment harder before you touch the model.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="PENALTY"><h4>Weight decay & dropout</h4><p>Weight decay (L2, decoupled à la AdamW) shrinks weights and smooths the landscape. Dropout randomly mutes units each step, forcing redundant representations. Both are cheap, both work, both deserve tuned rates — don't leave them at defaults forever.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="EARLY"><h4>Early stopping & ensembling</h4><p>Stop when validation loss plateaus — it is free regularization with a built-in model selection. Ensembling (multi-seed, multi-architecture, snapshot ensembles) is the highest-leverage "last 2%" before you ship.</p></div>
        <div class="card" data-glyph="ARCH"><h4>Architectural & data-based</h4><p>Smaller capacity, depthwise separable convs, knowledge distillation from a big teacher into a small student. And the quiet giant: <em>more, better data</em> beats most regularization tricks. Spend there first.</p></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">5.4</span>Diagnosing the two classic failures</h3>
      <div class="lost">
        <div class="lost-panel good rv">
          <h5>Underfitting — the model is too weak</h5>
          <svg viewBox="0 0 300 80" style="width:100%"><polyline points="0,60 30,58 60,55 90,50 120,44 150,38 180,32 210,27 240,23 270,20 300,18" fill="none" stroke="var(--ok)" stroke-width="2"/><text x="4" y="14" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="var(--ink-mute)">train & val both high, both still falling → capacity / features problem</text></svg>
          <p>Train and validation loss are both high and still descending. The model hasn't learned the structure. <strong>Fixes:</strong> more capacity, better features, longer training, higher LR, simpler preprocessing bugs. Check for bugs first — a loss that can't move is often a dead ReLU or a forgotten <code>optimizer.step()</code>.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="lost-panel bad rv" style="--d:.1s">
          <h5>Overfitting — the model is memorizing</h5>
          <svg viewBox="0 0 300 80" style="width:100%"><polyline points="0,14 30,20 60,30 90,40 120,50 150,57 180,62 210,65 240,67 270,68 300,69" fill="none" stroke="var(--ok)" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="0,14 30,18 60,24 90,30 120,38 150,48 180,58 210,52 240,44 270,38 300,33" fill="none" stroke="var(--bad)" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="4" y="72" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="var(--ink-mute)">train falls, validation rises → memorization</text></svg>
          <p>Train loss keeps falling while validation loss turns upward. The model is fitting noise. <strong>Fixes:</strong> more data, augmentation, dropout, weight decay, early stopping, smaller model. If the gap is huge, suspect label noise or leakage before anything else.</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">5.5</span>Pretraining & fine-tuning</h3>
      <p>The modern training stack is layered. <strong>Pretraining</strong> learns general representations from massive unlabeled (or self-supervised) data — next-token prediction for text, masked modeling for encoders, denoising for diffusion. <strong>Fine-tuning</strong> adapts those frozen-or-unfrozen weights to your task with far less data. <strong>Parameter-efficient variants</strong> — LoRA (low-rank adapters), prefix tuning, adapters — update a small fraction of the weights and make large-model adaptation practical on a single GPU. The rule of thumb: freeze the backbone, tune the head, add LoRA only when you need the capacity. And <strong>RLHF / DPO</strong> layers preference learning on top for behavior, not just accuracy.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="subblock rv">
      <h3><span class="hn">5.6</span>Scaling, hardware, and the practicalities of big training</h3>
      <ul class="dash">
        <li><strong>Mixed precision (FP16 / BF16)</strong> — halves memory and roughly doubles throughput; BF16 is the safe default for large transformers, with loss scaling for FP16.</li>
        <li><strong>Gradient accumulation</strong> — simulate a larger batch when the GPU can't hold it; mathematically equivalent (modulo batch-norm nuances).</li>
        <li><strong>Distributed strategies</strong> — data parallelism (shard batches), tensor parallelism (shard layers), pipeline parallelism (shard stages), and ZeRO/FSDP (shard optimizer state and parameters). Choose by where your memory bottleneck is.</li>
        <li><strong>Checkpointing & fault tolerance</strong> — at scale, hardware <em>will</em> fail mid-run. Async checkpoints, elastic re-launch, and deterministic replay are part of the architecture, not an afterthought.</li>
        <li><strong>Scaling laws</strong> — loss scales as a power law in model size, dataset size, and compute (Chinchilla: match tokens to parameters ~20:1). Use them to decide the shape of your budget before you spend it.</li>
        <li><strong>Reproducibility</strong> — pin seeds, log everything (W&B / MLflow), version data and code. A run you can't reproduce is a run you can't defend.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="exercise rv">
      <span class="etag">Exercise 05</span>
      <ol>
        <li>Run an LR range test on a small CNN. Plot loss vs. LR and identify the no-divergence point.</li>
        <li>Train the same net with and without warmup + cosine decay. Measure final validation loss and how many steps to 90% of the way there.</li>
        <li>Introduce deliberate overfitting (tiny batch, high LR, no decay). Then fix it with one technique at a time and record which single change closed the train/val gap the most.</li>
      </ol>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ======================= MODULE 06 · PIPELINE ======================= -->
<section class="chapter" id="pipeline">
  <div class="wrap">
    <header class="chapter-head rv">
      <span class="kicker">Module 06 — Beyond Training</span>
      <h2>A model isn't finished when it <em>trains</em>. It's finished when it's trusted.</h2>
      <p class="lede">The final mile is where most projects actually die — not in the loss curve, but in the deployment, the drift, the stakeholder meeting, and the 2 a.m. incident. Six stages stand between a checkpoint and a dependable system.</p>
    </header>

    <div class="subblock">
      <div class="stage rv"><span class="snum">01</span><h5>Evaluation & model selection</h5><p>Lock the test set. Run the full metric suite — lead metric, slices, calibration, latency, cost. Select the checkpoint by validation performance <em>only</em>, then report test once. If you look at test repeatedly, it becomes validation; you need a fresh holdout, which is why many teams keep a "gold" set that is scored exactly twice.</p><div class="stags"><span>holdout discipline</span><span>slice report</span><span>latency / cost</span></div></div>
      <div class="stage rv" style="--d:.05s"><span class="snum">02</span><h5>Optimization & packaging</h5><p>Export to ONNX or a runtime format, quantize (INT8 / INT4) where accuracy holds, prune or distill if the serving budget is tight, and bake the preprocessing into the artifact. The model and its transforms ship as one unit — a model file without its scaler is a promise without a contract.</p><div class="stags"><span>ONNX / TorchScript</span><span>quantization</span><span>distillation</span></div></div>
      <div class="stage rv" style="--d:.1s"><span class="snum">03</span><h5>Serving & inference</h5><p>Choose the topology: REST for simple requests, streaming for generation, batch for offline scoring. Batch aggressively — GPU utilization scales with batch size until latency dies. Set timeouts, rate limits, and a graceful fallback (cached answer, smaller model, human queue) for when the fast path fails.</p><div class="stags"><span>batching</span><span>streaming</span><span>fallback path</span></div></div>
      <div class="stage rv" style="--d:.15s"><span class="snum">04</span><h5>Monitoring & drift</h5><p>Track three families of signals: <em>input drift</em> (feature distributions vs. training), <em>prediction drift</em> (score distribution over time), and <em>outcome drift</em> (do labels still arrive, and does the model still predict them well?). Alert on PSI or KL divergence per feature; retrain triggers should be defined in advance, not invented in the incident channel.</p><div class="stags"><span>PSI / KL drift</span><span>score monitoring</span><span>outcome feedback loop</span></div></div>
      <div class="stage rv" style="--d:.2s"><span class="snum">05</span><h5>Retraining & lifecycle</h5><p>Schedule retraining on data freshness, not calendar convenience. Version every artifact (model, data, code, config) as a single deployable unit. Keep the last known-good checkpoint hot for instant rollback, and automate the champion/challenger comparison so a new model must <em>beat</em> the old one on the live eval set before it earns production.</p><div class="stags"><span>champion / challenger</span><span>rollback</span><span>artifact versioning</span></div></div>
      <div class="stage rv" style="--d:.25s"><span class="snum">06</span><h5>Governance & continuous audit</h5><p>Maintain the model card: intended use, known limitations, slice performance, and rollback owner. Run periodic fairness and safety audits, especially after any data or model change. Treat the model as a regulated surface — the same review rigor you'd give a payment system, scaled to its actual blast radius.</p><div class="stags"><span>model card</span><span>fairness audit</span><span>incident owner</span></div></div>
    </div>

    <div class="callout key rv"><span class="ct">The MLOps loop, in one sentence</span><p>Capture → curate → train → evaluate → deploy → monitor → detect drift → re-capture. The loop, not the model, is the product.</p></div>

    <div class="exercise rv">
      <span class="etag">Exercise 06</span>
      <ol>
        <li>Wrap your trained model in a FastAPI endpoint with a request validator and a 200 ms p95 budget. Load-test it and find where the bottleneck actually is.</li>
        <li>Compute PSI between your training features and the last 7 days of (simulated) production features. Which feature drifted most?</li>
        <li>Write the model card for your system in under 300 words. You will be amazed what you don't yet know about it.</li>
      </ol>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

    <span>Curriculum · Cohort 2025</span>
    <span>Set in Fraunces & IBM Plex · Built as one HTML file</span>
  </div>
</footer>

<button class="totop" id="toTop" aria-label="Back to top">
  <svg width="16" height="16" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M12 19V5M5 12l7-7 7 7"/></svg>
</button>

<script>
/* ============================================================
   CURRICULUM — behavior
   ============================================================ */
(function(){
  "use strict";
  const root = document.documentElement;

  /* ---------- theme toggle ---------- */
  const toggle = document.getElementById('themeToggle');
  function syncToggle(){
    const light = root.dataset.theme === 'light';
    toggle.setAttribute('aria-checked', light ? 'true' : 'false');
    toggle.setAttribute('aria-label', light ? 'Switch to dark theme' : 'Switch to light theme');
  }
  toggle.addEventListener('click', () => {
    const next = root.dataset.theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark';
    root.dataset.theme = next;
    try{ localStorage.setItem('theme', next); }catch(e){}
    syncToggle();
  });
  syncToggle();

  /* ---------- hero neural network (generated + animated) ---------- */
  const net = document.getElementById('netSvg');
  const layers = [4, 6, 6, 3];
  const W = 520, H = 340, padX = 42, padY = 34;
  const cols = layers.length;
  const xs = layers.map((_, i) => padX + i * (W - 2*padX) / (cols - 1));
  const nodes = [];
  layers.forEach((n, li) => {
    for(let j = 0; j < n; j++){
      const y = padY + j * (H - 2*padY) / (n - 1);
      nodes.push({x: xs[li], y, li, j, id: 'n'+li+'_'+j});
    }
  });
  const byLayer = layers.map((_, li) => nodes.filter(n => n.li === li));
  let svg = '';
  // edges
  for(let li = 0; li < cols - 1; li++){
    byLayer[li].forEach(a => byLayer[li+1].forEach(b => {
      svg += '<line class="edge" data-a="'+a.id+'" data-b="'+b.id+'" x1="'+a.x+'" y1="'+a.y+'" x2="'+b.x+'" y2="'+b.y+'"/>';
    }));
  }
  // pulse paths (a few sampled edges for traveling pulses)
  const picks = [];
  for(let li = 0; li < cols - 1; li++){
    const a = byLayer[li][Math.floor(Math.random()*byLayer[li].length)];
    const b = byLayer[li+1][Math.floor(Math.random()*byLayer[li+1].length)];
    picks.push({a,b,li});
  }
  picks.forEach((p,i) => {
    svg += '<circle class="pulse" id="p'+i+'" r="3.4" cx="'+p.a.x+'" cy="'+p.a.y+'" style="animation-delay:'+(i*0.55)+'s"><animate attributeName="cx" from="'+p.a.x+'" to="'+p.b.x+'" dur="2.4s" repeatCount="indefinite" begin="'+(i*0.55)+'s"/><animate attributeName="cy" from="'+p.a.y+'" to="'+p.b.y+'" dur="2.4s" repeatCount="indefinite" begin="'+(i*0.55)+'s"/></circle>';
  });
  // nodes
  nodes.forEach(n => { svg += '<circle class="node" id="'+n.id+'" cx="'+n.x+'" cy="'+n.y+'" r="'+(n.li===0||n.li===cols-1?8:6)+'"/>'; });
  net.innerHTML = svg;

  const allNodes = [...net.querySelectorAll('.node')];
  const allEdges = [...net.querySelectorAll('.edge')];
  function flash(){
    // light up a random path
    const path = [];
    let cur = byLayer[0][Math.floor(Math.random()*byLayer[0].length)];
    path.push(cur);
    for(let li = 1; li < cols; li++){
      cur = byLayer[li][Math.floor(Math.random()*byLayer[li].length)];
      path.push(cur);
    }
    const hotE = new Set();
    for(let i = 0; i < path.length - 1; i++){
      const e = allEdges.find(l => l.dataset.a === path[i].id && l.dataset.b === path[i+1].id);
      if(e) hotE.add(e);
    }
    path.forEach((n, i) => {
      setTimeout(() => n.classList.add('hot'), i * 120);
    });
    hotE.forEach(e => e.classList.add('hot'));
    setTimeout(() => {
      allNodes.forEach(n => n.classList.remove('hot'));
      allEdges.forEach(e => e.classList.remove('hot'));
    }, path.length * 120 + 350);
  }
  let flashTimer = null;
  function startFlash(){
    if (window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches) return;
    if (flashTimer) return;
    flashTimer = setInterval(flash, 1400);
    flash();
  }
  function stopFlash(){ clearInterval(flashTimer); flashTimer = null; }
  const heroIO = new IntersectionObserver(es => {
    es.forEach(e => e.isIntersecting ? startFlash() : stopFlash());
  }, {threshold:.15});
  heroIO.observe(document.querySelector('.hero'));

  /* ---------- reading progress ---------- */
  const fill = document.getElementById('readFill');
  const pct  = document.getElementById('readPct');
  const toTop = document.getElementById('toTop');
  function onScroll(){
    const doc = document.documentElement;
    const max = doc.scrollHeight - doc.clientHeight;
    const p = max > 0 ? Math.min(1, doc.scrollTop / max) : 0;
    fill.style.width = (p * 100).toFixed(1) + '%';
    pct.textContent = Math.round(p * 100) + '%';
    toTop.classList.toggle('show', doc.scrollTop > 600);
  }
  document.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, {passive:true});
  onScroll();
  toTop.addEventListener('click', () => window.scrollTo({top:0, behavior:'smooth'}));

  /* ---------- reveal on scroll ---------- */
  const rvEls = document.querySelectorAll('.rv');
  const rvIO = new IntersectionObserver(es => {
    es.forEach(e => { if(e.isIntersecting){ e.target.classList.add('on'); rvIO.unobserve(e.target); } });
  }, {threshold:.12, rootMargin:'0px 0px -40px 0px'});
  rvEls.forEach(el => rvIO.observe(el));

  /* ---------- rail active state ---------- */
  const secs = [...document.querySelectorAll('.chapter, .hero')].filter(s => s.id);
  const railLinks = [...document.querySelectorAll('.rail a')];
  const secIO = new IntersectionObserver(es => {
    es.forEach(e => {
      if(e.isIntersecting){
        railLinks.forEach(a => a.classList.toggle('active', a.dataset.sec === e.target.id));
      }
    });
  }, {rootMargin:'-40% 0px -55% 0px'});
  secs.forEach(s => secIO.observe(s));

  /* ---------- precision / recall gauge ---------- */
  const TP = 900, FP = 99100; // population
  // synthetic score distributions: positives ~ N(0.62, 0.24), negatives ~ N(0.30, 0.20)
  function cdf(x, mu, sd){ // standard normal cdf via erf approx
    const z = (x - mu) / sd;
    const t = 1 / (1 + 0.2316419 * Math.abs(z));
    const d = 0.3989423 * Math.exp(-z*z/2);
    let p = d * t * (0.3193815 + t * (-0.3565638 + t * (1.781478 + t * (-1.821256 + t * 1.330274))));
    return z > 0 ? 1 - p : p;
  }
  const gTh = document.getElementById('gTh');
  const gThOut = document.getElementById('gThOut');
  const gRecall = document.getElementById('gRecall');
  const gRecallVal = document.getElementById('gRecallVal');
  const gPrecLabel = document.getElementById('gPrecLabel');
  const gTP = document.getElementById('gTP');
  const gFP = document.getElementById('gFP');
  const gF1 = document.getElementById('gF1');
  const gNote = document.getElementById('gNote');
  const ARC = 409; // arc length of the r=130 semicircle: π·130 ≈ 408.4
  function fmt(n){ return n.toLocaleString('en-US'); }
  function updateGauge(){
    const t = parseFloat(gTh.value);
    gThOut.textContent = t.toFixed(2);
    const recall = 1 - cdf(t, 0.62, 0.24);  // P(pos score > t)
    const fpr    = 1 - cdf(t, 0.30, 0.20);  // P(neg score > t)
    const tp = Math.round(recall * TP);
    const fp = Math.round(fpr * FP);
    const prec = tp + fp > 0 ? tp / (tp + fp) : 0;
    const f1 = prec + recall > 0 ? 2 * prec * recall / (prec + recall) : 0;
    gRecallVal.textContent = (recall * 100).toFixed(1) + '%';
    gRecall.style.strokeDashoffset = ARC * (1 - recall);
    gPrecLabel.textContent = 'Precision ' + (prec * 100 < 0.1 && prec > 0 ? prec * 100 < 0.01 ? '<0.1%' : (prec*100).toFixed(1)+'%' : (prec*100).toFixed(1) + '%');
    gTP.textContent = fmt(tp);
    gFP.textContent = fmt(fp);
    gF1.textContent = f1.toFixed(3);
    let note;
    if (t < 0.35) note = 'Threshold ' + t.toFixed(2) + ' — you catch almost everything, but the false-alarm bill (' + fmt(fp) + ' clean transactions) dwarfs the frauds. Recall is cheap here; trust is not.';
    else if (t < 0.6) note = 'Threshold ' + t.toFixed(2) + ' — catching ' + (recall*100).toFixed(0) + '% of frauds while flagging ' + fmt(fp) + ' clean cases. The classic operating point: high recall, painful precision.';
    else if (t < 0.8) note = 'Threshold ' + t.toFixed(2) + ' — false alarms drop to ' + fmt(fp) + ', but you now miss ' + ((1-recall)*100).toFixed(0) + '% of real fraud. Precision rises; recall pays for it.';
    else note = 'Threshold ' + t.toFixed(2) + ' — precision is finally respectable, yet you catch only ' + (recall*100).toFixed(1) + '% of frauds. This is the trade no metric alone can resolve — only your business cost function can.';
    gNote.innerHTML = note.replace('you catch almost everything', '<b>you catch almost everything</b>').replace('The classic operating point', '<b>The classic operating point</b>');
  }
  gTh.addEventListener('input', updateGauge);
  // animate gauge in when visible
  const gBlock = document.getElementById('gaugeBlock');
  const gIO = new IntersectionObserver(es => {
    es.forEach(e => { if(e.isIntersecting){ gBlock.classList.add('on'); gIO.unobserve(e.target); } });
  }, {threshold:.2});
  if(gBlock) gIO.observe(gBlock);
  updateGauge();
})();
</script>
</body>
