/* ============================================================
   CURRICULUM — behavior
   ============================================================ */
(function(){
  "use strict";
  const root = document.documentElement;

  /* ---------- theme toggle ---------- */
  const toggle = document.getElementById('themeToggle');
  function syncToggle(){
    const light = root.dataset.theme === 'light';
    toggle.setAttribute('aria-checked', light ? 'true' : 'false');
    toggle.setAttribute('aria-label', light ? 'Switch to dark theme' : 'Switch to light theme');
  }
  toggle.addEventListener('click', () => {
    const next = root.dataset.theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark';
    root.dataset.theme = next;
    try{ localStorage.setItem('theme', next); }catch(e){}
    syncToggle();
  });
  syncToggle();

  /* ---------- hero neural network (generated + animated) ---------- */
  const net = document.getElementById('netSvg');
  const layers = [4, 6, 6, 3];
  const W = 520, H = 340, padX = 42, padY = 34;
  const cols = layers.length;
  const xs = layers.map((_, i) => padX + i * (W - 2*padX) / (cols - 1));
  const nodes = [];
  layers.forEach((n, li) => {
    for(let j = 0; j < n; j++){
      const y = padY + j * (H - 2*padY) / (n - 1);
      nodes.push({x: xs[li], y, li, j, id: 'n'+li+'_'+j});
    }
  });
  const byLayer = layers.map((_, li) => nodes.filter(n => n.li === li));
  let svg = '';
  // edges
  for(let li = 0; li < cols - 1; li++){
    byLayer[li].forEach(a => byLayer[li+1].forEach(b => {
      svg += '<line class="edge" data-a="'+a.id+'" data-b="'+b.id+'" x1="'+a.x+'" y1="'+a.y+'" x2="'+b.x+'" y2="'+b.y+'"/>';
    }));
  }
  // pulse paths (a few sampled edges for traveling pulses)
  const picks = [];
  for(let li = 0; li < cols - 1; li++){
    const a = byLayer[li][Math.floor(Math.random()*byLayer[li].length)];
    const b = byLayer[li+1][Math.floor(Math.random()*byLayer[li+1].length)];
    picks.push({a,b,li});
  }
  picks.forEach((p,i) => {
    svg += '<circle class="pulse" id="p'+i+'" r="3.4" cx="'+p.a.x+'" cy="'+p.a.y+'" style="animation-delay:'+(i*0.55)+'s"><animate attributeName="cx" from="'+p.a.x+'" to="'+p.b.x+'" dur="2.4s" repeatCount="indefinite" begin="'+(i*0.55)+'s"/><animate attributeName="cy" from="'+p.a.y+'" to="'+p.b.y+'" dur="2.4s" repeatCount="indefinite" begin="'+(i*0.55)+'s"/></circle>';
  });
  // nodes
  nodes.forEach(n => { svg += '<circle class="node" id="'+n.id+'" cx="'+n.x+'" cy="'+n.y+'" r="'+(n.li===0||n.li===cols-1?8:6)+'"/>'; });
  net.innerHTML = svg;

  const allNodes = [...net.querySelectorAll('.node')];
  const allEdges = [...net.querySelectorAll('.edge')];
  function flash(){
    // light up a random path
    const path = [];
    let cur = byLayer[0][Math.floor(Math.random()*byLayer[0].length)];
    path.push(cur);
    for(let li = 1; li < cols; li++){
      cur = byLayer[li][Math.floor(Math.random()*byLayer[li].length)];
      path.push(cur);
    }
    const hotE = new Set();
    for(let i = 0; i < path.length - 1; i++){
      const e = allEdges.find(l => l.dataset.a === path[i].id && l.dataset.b === path[i+1].id);
      if(e) hotE.add(e);
    }
    path.forEach((n, i) => {
      setTimeout(() => n.classList.add('hot'), i * 120);
    });
    hotE.forEach(e => e.classList.add('hot'));
    setTimeout(() => {
      allNodes.forEach(n => n.classList.remove('hot'));
      allEdges.forEach(e => e.classList.remove('hot'));
    }, path.length * 120 + 350);
  }
  let flashTimer = null;
  function startFlash(){
    if (window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches) return;
    if (flashTimer) return;
    flashTimer = setInterval(flash, 1400);
    flash();
  }
  function stopFlash(){ clearInterval(flashTimer); flashTimer = null; }
  const heroIO = new IntersectionObserver(es => {
    es.forEach(e => e.isIntersecting ? startFlash() : stopFlash());
  }, {threshold:.15});
  heroIO.observe(document.querySelector('.hero'));

  /* ---------- reading progress ---------- */
  const fill = document.getElementById('readFill');
  const pct  = document.getElementById('readPct');
  const toTop = document.getElementById('toTop');
  function onScroll(){
    const doc = document.documentElement;
    const max = doc.scrollHeight - doc.clientHeight;
    const p = max > 0 ? Math.min(1, doc.scrollTop / max) : 0;
    fill.style.width = (p * 100).toFixed(1) + '%';
    pct.textContent = Math.round(p * 100) + '%';
    toTop.classList.toggle('show', doc.scrollTop > 600);
  }
  document.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, {passive:true});
  onScroll();
  toTop.addEventListener('click', () => window.scrollTo({top:0, behavior:'smooth'}));

  /* ---------- reveal on scroll ---------- */
  const rvEls = document.querySelectorAll('.rv');
  const rvIO = new IntersectionObserver(es => {
    es.forEach(e => { if(e.isIntersecting){ e.target.classList.add('on'); rvIO.unobserve(e.target); } });
  }, {threshold:.12, rootMargin:'0px 0px -40px 0px'});
  rvEls.forEach(el => rvIO.observe(el));

  /* ---------- rail active state ---------- */
  const secs = [...document.querySelectorAll('.chapter, .hero')].filter(s => s.id);
  const railLinks = [...document.querySelectorAll('.rail a')];
  const secIO = new IntersectionObserver(es => {
    es.forEach(e => {
      if(e.isIntersecting){
        railLinks.forEach(a => a.classList.toggle('active', a.dataset.sec === e.target.id));
      }
    });
  }, {rootMargin:'-40% 0px -55% 0px'});
  secs.forEach(s => secIO.observe(s));

  /* ---------- precision / recall gauge ---------- */
  const TP = 900, FP = 99100; // population
  // synthetic score distributions: positives ~ N(0.62, 0.24), negatives ~ N(0.30, 0.20)
  function cdf(x, mu, sd){ // standard normal cdf via erf approx
    const z = (x - mu) / sd;
    const t = 1 / (1 + 0.2316419 * Math.abs(z));
    const d = 0.3989423 * Math.exp(-z*z/2);
    let p = d * t * (0.3193815 + t * (-0.3565638 + t * (1.781478 + t * (-1.821256 + t * 1.330274))));
    return z > 0 ? 1 - p : p;
  }
  const gTh = document.getElementById('gTh');
  const gThOut = document.getElementById('gThOut');
  const gRecall = document.getElementById('gRecall');
  const gRecallVal = document.getElementById('gRecallVal');
  const gPrecLabel = document.getElementById('gPrecLabel');
  const gTP = document.getElementById('gTP');
  const gFP = document.getElementById('gFP');
  const gF1 = document.getElementById('gF1');
  const gNote = document.getElementById('gNote');
  const ARC = 409; // arc length of the r=130 semicircle: π·130 ≈ 408.4
  function fmt(n){ return n.toLocaleString('en-US'); }
  function updateGauge(){
    const t = parseFloat(gTh.value);
    gThOut.textContent = t.toFixed(2);
    const recall = 1 - cdf(t, 0.62, 0.24);  // P(pos score > t)
    const fpr    = 1 - cdf(t, 0.30, 0.20);  // P(neg score > t)
    const tp = Math.round(recall * TP);
    const fp = Math.round(fpr * FP);
    const prec = tp + fp > 0 ? tp / (tp + fp) : 0;
    const f1 = prec + recall > 0 ? 2 * prec * recall / (prec + recall) : 0;
    gRecallVal.textContent = (recall * 100).toFixed(1) + '%';
    gRecall.style.strokeDashoffset = ARC * (1 - recall);
    gPrecLabel.textContent = 'Precision ' + (prec * 100 < 0.1 && prec > 0 ? prec * 100 < 0.01 ? '<0.1%' : (prec*100).toFixed(1)+'%' : (prec*100).toFixed(1) + '%');
    gTP.textContent = fmt(tp);
    gFP.textContent = fmt(fp);
    gF1.textContent = f1.toFixed(3);
    let note;
    if (t < 0.35) note = 'Threshold ' + t.toFixed(2) + ' — you catch almost everything, but the false-alarm bill (' + fmt(fp) + ' clean transactions) dwarfs the frauds. Recall is cheap here; trust is not.';
    else if (t < 0.6) note = 'Threshold ' + t.toFixed(2) + ' — catching ' + (recall*100).toFixed(0) + '% of frauds while flagging ' + fmt(fp) + ' clean cases. The classic operating point: high recall, painful precision.';
    else if (t < 0.8) note = 'Threshold ' + t.toFixed(2) + ' — false alarms drop to ' + fmt(fp) + ', but you now miss ' + ((1-recall)*100).toFixed(0) + '% of real fraud. Precision rises; recall pays for it.';
    else note = 'Threshold ' + t.toFixed(2) + ' — precision is finally respectable, yet you catch only ' + (recall*100).toFixed(1) + '% of frauds. This is the trade no metric alone can resolve — only your business cost function can.';
    gNote.innerHTML = note.replace('you catch almost everything', '<b>you catch almost everything</b>').replace('The classic operating point', '<b>The classic operating point</b>');
  }
  gTh.addEventListener('input', updateGauge);
  // animate gauge in when visible
  const gBlock = document.getElementById('gaugeBlock');
  const gIO = new IntersectionObserver(es => {
    es.forEach(e => { if(e.isIntersecting){ gBlock.classList.add('on'); gIO.unobserve(e.target); } });
  }, {threshold:.2});
  if(gBlock) gIO.observe(gBlock);
  updateGauge();
})();
</script>
</body>
</html>

A Field Course

Curriculum

in Creating AI Models

Network Architectures · Data Preparation · Metrics · Training Methods

Seven Chapters · Six Exercises

Single-file edition · 2025

Contents

  1. Preface — How to Use This Book
  2. Chapter 1 — FoundationsWhat a model actually is · the three learning paradigms · loss, gradients, and the training loop · choosing the right tool
  3. Chapter 2 — ArchitecturesLinear models and MLPs · CNNs · RNNs · attention and transformers · generative models · ensembles · a decision rubric
  4. Chapter 3 — Data PreparationThe seven-stage pipeline · labeling and agreement · leakage-proof splits · quality audits · the ethics layer
  5. Chapter 4 — MetricsThe confusion matrix · precision, recall, Fβ · ROC versus PR · regression and NLP metrics · fairness and calibration · the threshold trade-off
  6. Chapter 5 — Training MethodsOptimizers · learning-rate strategy · regularization · underfitting versus overfitting · pretraining and fine-tuning · scaling laws and hardware
  7. Chapter 6 — Beyond TrainingEvaluation discipline · packaging and serving · drift monitoring · the retraining lifecycle · governance
  8. Chapter 7 — The Full SyllabusThe complete course at a glance · where to go from here
  9. Glossary
  10. Further Study
  11. Colophon

Preface — How to Use This Book

You are holding a compressed field course in creating AI models: seven chapters that take you from a single perceptron to a transformer trained on GPUs, and then past the loss curve to a monitored, governed production system. It assumes you can code a little and are willing to be precise about the rest. Everything else is taught in place.

The book is organized in four movements:

  • Chapters 1–2 establish what a model is and the shapes it can take — the vocabulary of architectures.
  • Chapters 3–4 cover the discipline around the model — data preparation and the measurement system that tells you whether it is any good.
  • Chapters 5–6 explain how models learn (optimization, regularization, scaling) and what happens after training (serving, drift, retraining, governance).
  • Chapter 7 lays the whole syllabus out at a glance, with a reading list and a path forward.

Six dashed boxes marked Exercise are woven through the chapters. They are not optional reading; they are the course. A model you have not trained yourself is a word you have only heard.

A note on editions

This file is the single source of truth for the book. In the web companion (Curriculum) the threshold trade-off in §4.6 is an interactive gauge you can drag; here it is a static table — same numbers, less friction. To convert this file into EPUB or MOBI, see the accompanying README, or run make_epub.py for a dependency-free build.

Chapter 1

Foundations

Every model is a function waiting to be shaped. Machine learning reframes a problem: instead of writing the rules, you write a parameterized function and let data determine its parameters.

1.1 What a model actually is

A model is a family of functions. A linear model is ŷ = w·x + b: the family is all lines, and the parameters (w, b) pick one specific line. A neural network is the same idea taken to the extreme — a function whose shape is so flexible that, given enough width and depth, it can approximate essentially any mapping. Training is the process of navigating parameter space until the function behaves the way you want. Everything else in this book — architectures, data pipelines, metrics — exists in service of that one act: fitting f(x) so that f(x) ≈ y.

In practice, building a model is a six-step workflow. Keep the shape of it in mind; every later chapter is a zoom into one of these steps.

  1. Collect. Raw signals — logs, images, text, sensor streams.
  2. Structure. Clean, label, and split into train / validation / test.
  3. Choose. Pick an architecture suited to the data (Chapter 2).
  4. Fit. Optimize parameters against a loss function (Chapter 5).
  5. Evaluate. Measure on held-out data. Iterate honestly (Chapter 4).
  6. Ship. Deploy, monitor, and retrain as the world shifts (Chapter 6).

1.2 The three learning paradigms

How does the model learn? Three regimes, distinguished by what signal the data provides:

ParadigmWhat the model seesWhere it shines
SupervisedLabeled pairs (x, y); the model is graded on every predictionClassification and regression — the workhorse of most applications, and the setting where most of this book lives
UnsupervisedUnlabeled data; the model must find structureClustering, embeddings, dimensionality reduction — and crucially, the self-supervised pretraining that powers modern AI
ReinforcementDelayed reward signals for sequences of actionsRobotics, game play, and preference-based alignment (RLHF) for language models
In practice

State-of-the-art systems rarely pick just one. A typical large language model is self-supervised (predict the next token) for most of its compute, then supervised fine-tuned on demonstrations, then reinforcement-tuned against human preferences. Paradigms stack; the fundamentals do not change.

1.3 Loss, gradients, and the engine of learning

Training needs three ingredients: a loss function that scores how wrong the model is, a differentiable path from parameters to that score, and an optimizer that walks the parameters downhill. The magic ingredient is the chain rule — backpropagation — which computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter in a single backward pass.

# the entire training loop, honestly compressed
for batch in dataloader:
    x, y = batch
    y_hat = model(x)              # forward pass
    loss  = criterion(y_hat, y)   # how wrong?
    loss.backward()               # backprop: ∂loss/∂θ
    optimizer.step()              # nudge parameters
    optimizer.zero_grad()

Autograd frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow) build a computation graph during the forward pass and apply the chain rule automatically. Your job is to design the graph; the framework does the calculus.

1.4 Choosing the right tool

Not every problem deserves a neural network. A first mapping from task shape to starting point:

Task shapeStart hereReach for instead
Structured table, clean columnsGradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM)Logistic / linear regression, small MLPs
Images, video, raw pixelsConvolutional networksViT-style transformers, diffusion models
Text and languageA pretrained transformerFine-tune an LLM — a smaller one first
Sequences with local patternsRNN / GRU / small CNNTransformer encoder (attention wins at scale)
Decisions over timeValue methods, policy gradientsPPO with a learned reward model
Exercise 01
  1. Take the iris dataset and fit sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression.
  2. Print coef_ and intercept_ — these are the learned function. Which feature dominates for each class?
  3. Now fit the same model on 30 samples. Compare the coefficients. What does that instability teach you about data scale?

Chapter 2

Architectures

The anatomy of a model: classifiers to transformers. An architecture is a bet about structure — each family assumes something about how the data is organized, and encodes that assumption in its wiring.

2.1 Linear models and the perceptron

The perceptron is the atom of deep learning: a dot product plus a threshold. Keep it linear and you have regression; stack layers of it and you have a network. Linear models remain a first resort because they are interpretable — each weight is a direct statement about a feature — and they anchor the intuition: every nonlinearity you add later is a controlled departure from this simple case.

They endure for good reasons: fast to fit, cheap to serve, no hyperparameter maze, and coefficients that read like a report. Logistic regression is still the baseline that deep models must beat to earn their GPU time. But a straight hyperplane cannot carve XOR-shaped decision boundaries, and the feature engineering needed to bend it becomes unmanageable. That gap is exactly what nonlinear models exist to fill.

2.2 Feedforward networks (MLPs)

A multilayer perceptron chains a small set of operations, repeated:

  1. Input. A raw feature vector x ∈ ℝⁿ — flattened, scaled, ready.
  2. Linear. z = Wx + b — a learned projection into a new geometry.
  3. Nonlinear. σ(z) — ReLU or GELU. Without it, stacking layers is just one big matrix multiplication.
  4. Normalize. BatchNorm or LayerNorm — keeps activations in a trainable range.
  5. Head. The task output — class logits, a scalar, or a probability vector.

The universal approximation theorem says one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function — in practice you need many layers, which is why the field went deep. The subtlety: more layers and width buy expressivity, but only the right initialization, normalization, and optimizer make that capacity learnable. Architecture is a contract between capacity and optimization.

2.3 CNNs — vision's local experts

Convolutional networks encode a powerful prior: locality and translation invariance. Kernels slide across the input, reusing the same weights, building edge → texture → part → object hierarchies while pooling layers shrink spatial dimensions and enlarge receptive fields.

ComponentWhat it doesWhy it matters
Conv layerSliding kernel extracts local featuresWeight sharing — orders of magnitude fewer parameters than a dense layer on images
PoolingDownsamples (max / avg / strided conv)Grows receptive field, adds robustness to small shifts
BatchNormNormalizes activations per mini-batchStabilizes training, allows higher learning rates
Residual skipy = F(x) + x (ResNet)Gradients flow unimpeded → networks with 100+ layers
Global avg poolCollapses spatial dims to a vectorBridges the visual stack to a classification head
Lineage worth knowing

LeNet (1998) → AlexNet (2012) → VGG / GoogLeNet / ResNet (2014–15) → EfficientNet (2019). Each step was less about a new idea and more about training a bigger one reliably: better initialization, normalization, and skip connections did as much as any structural novelty.

2.4 RNNs — memory as state

Recurrent networks process sequences step by step, carrying a hidden state hₜ = tanh(W·hₜ₋₁ + U·xₜ). Elegant, but the same matrix is multiplied t times, so gradients shrink or explode along the path. LSTMs added a gated cell state that can hold information across long spans; GRUs simplified the gate structure. For short, tightly local sequences they remain light and effective; for long-range dependencies, attention won.

2.5 Attention and transformers

The transformer replaced recurrence with attention: every position can read every other position directly, in parallel. The mechanism is three learned projections — Query, Key, Value — compared pairwise:

# multi-head attention in four lines
Q, K, V = Wq x, Wk x, Wv x              # projections
scores  = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k)           # similarity matrix
attn    = softmax(scores, dim=-1)       # weight the values
out     = attn @ V                      # weighted combination

The encoder block assembles the pieces: input + positional encoding → self-attention (every token reads all tokens) → a two-layer feedforward net applied per position → residual connections + LayerNorm for stable gradients → repeat for N layers → task head. Stack N of them, scale the dimension d, and you get the same machine that powers modern language, vision, and multimodal models. The architecture has been stable since 2017; the scale and data are what changed.

  • Encoder-only (BERT-style): bidirectional context → understanding tasks, embeddings, classification.
  • Decoder-only (GPT-style): causal mask, next-token prediction → the dominant architecture for generative LLMs.
  • Encoder–decoder (T5 / the original): read with an encoder, generate with a decoder → translation and summarization.
Why attention scaled

Recurrence forces a serial chain of length t; attention computes all pairwise relations at once and parallelizes perfectly on GPUs. The cost is O(t²) memory — which is why modern work keeps reinventing efficient attention (sliding windows, sparsity, linear approximations) rather than abandoning it.

2.6 Generative models

A distinct family of architectures aims not to classify but to produce — images, audio, text. Four mechanisms dominate:

FamilyCore ideaTrade-off
GANsA generator and discriminator play a min-max game until fakes become indistinguishable from realPowerful but notoriously unstable; mode collapse is the classic failure
VAEsMatch an encoder's output to a Gaussian prior, learning a smooth probabilistic latent spaceSofter samples, but the most principled latent geometry — and a natural regularizer
DiffusionNoisify data to pure noise, then train a network to reverse the process; iterate the reversal to sampleThe current king of high-fidelity image synthesis; slower at inference
AutoregressiveModel P(x) = Π P(xᵢ | x<ᵢ): predict the next element, append it, repeatSimple and flexible — via the transformer decoder, the engine of modern text generation

2.7 Ensembles and tree methods

Not everything is a neural net. Random forests average many decorrelated trees (bagging); gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) sequences trees, each correcting its predecessor's residuals. On tabular data they remain a formidable baseline — often beating neural networks with a fraction of the engineering. A useful rule: a model that a well-tuned ensemble cannot improve is a model you can trust.

2.8 Choosing an architecture — a decision rubric

QuestionIf…Then lean toward
What modality?Images / videoCNN, ViT, diffusion
Text / languageTransformer (decoder-only for generation)
Tabular dataBoosted trees first, MLP second
How much data?Under ~10⁴ labeled rowsSimple models + strong features; deep nets overfit
10⁶+ samples or tokensDeep networks and pretraining pay off
Latency budget?Milliseconds, edge deviceSmall CNN, distilled model, or trees
Server-side, batchedBig transformers are affordable
Interpretability?Required for complianceLinear models or trees; probe-based explanations for nets
Exercise 02
  1. Train a 2-layer MLP and a 6-layer MLP (with residual connections) on MNIST. Plot train and validation loss for both.
  2. Remove the nonlinearity from the 6-layer net. Watch what happens — and explain why in one sentence.
  3. Now compare gradient norms across layers with and without the skip connection. What did the residual do?

Chapter 3

Data Preparation

Data preparation is the real model. There is a quiet law of the field: models commoditize, data doesn't.

3.1 The seven-stage pipeline

  1. Collection and sourcing. Define the target population precisely; data collected outside it is confidently wrong. Document provenance — you will need it for audits.
  2. Cleaning and deduplication. Fix malformed records, collapse exact and near-duplicates, reconcile units and timezones. Duplicates are silent label-leakage factories.
  3. Labeling. The most expensive stage. Write a labeling rubric before hiring labelers, compute inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ or Krippendorff's α), and route disagreements to adjudication. Your label noise sets the ceiling on achievable accuracy — no model escapes it.
  4. Feature engineering. Encoding (one-hot, target, embeddings), scaling, aggregations, windowed statistics for sequences. For text: tokenization and vocabulary design. For images: resizing, crops, color space.
  5. Splitting. Hold out validation and test sets before any modeling decision. For temporal data: split by time, never randomly. For grouped data: split by group, or you leak.
  6. Balancing and weighting. Address class imbalance with stratification, resampling, or loss weighting — and decide whether the model should optimize accuracy or cost (Chapter 4 explains why these differ).
  7. Packaging and versioning. Ship datasets as versioned artifacts (DVC, LakeFS, HF Datasets) with a schema, a hash, and a changelog. Reproducibility is a data problem before it is a code problem.

Where does the time actually go? In a typical industrial project, by engineer-hours:

StageShare of effort
Labeling≈ 44%
Cleaning≈ 21%
QA and audit≈ 14%
Splitting≈ 9%
Packaging≈ 7%
Sourcing≈ 5%

Training itself is rarely the bottleneck.

3.2 The preprocessing patterns that repeat everywhere

ProblemStandard treatmentClassic failure
Missing valuesImpute (median / model-based) or add explicit missing-indicator featuresImputing on the full set before splitting leaks test information into train
Scale mismatchStandardize / min-max, fitted on train only, applied to val/testScaling on all data — a subtle, pervasive leak
High-cardinality categoricalsTarget encoding (with smoothing / CV) or learned embeddingsNaive target encoding overfits; one-hot explodes dimensionality
Class imbalanceStratified splits, class weights, focal loss, targeted resamplingRandom resampling duplicates patterns and inflates confidence
Temporal dataTime-ordered splits, embargo gaps, walk-forward validationRandom splits that let the model peek at "future" rows
TextTokenization, vocabulary / BPE, truncation or windowingTraining and inference using different tokenizers
ImagesResize + random crops/flips (train), center crop (test); augmentationApplying test-time transforms only at train time
The cardinal rule

Every statistic you compute — means, frequencies, encodings, scaler parameters — must be derived from training data only, then applied to validation and test. Fit on the fold, transform everything. Frameworks like scikit-learn's Pipeline and cross_val_score exist to make this hard to get wrong. Use them.

3.3 Data quality: the audits that save you

  • Distribution drift check. Compare feature distributions across time slices; a silent shift in production is the most common cause of "the model degraded overnight."
  • Label audit. Sample 200 labeled examples, re-label blind, measure agreement. Below κ ≈ 0.6, fix the rubric, not the model.
  • Nearest-neighbor dedup. Embedding-based kNN over the corpus to surface near-duplicates across train/val/test boundaries.
  • Outlier profiling. Isolation Forest or per-feature z-score review; decide per feature whether to clip, keep, or drop.
  • Representation check. Train a small probe on the frozen features; if the probe cannot separate the classes, the features (or the labels) are broken.

3.4 The ethics layer

Preparation is also where bias is introduced or prevented. Four questions before a dataset ships:

  • Who is missing? Coverage across demographics, regions, and languages — absence in data is absence in service.
  • Whose labels? Labeler demographics and rubric framing shape what the model considers "normal."
  • Consent and rights. Is the source licensed, is PII redacted, does the data contain biometric or health information with special legal status?
  • Harm surface. Who bears the cost when this model is wrong, and is that cost symmetric across groups? Run a group-wise fairness slice (Chapter 4) before launch.
Exercise 03
  1. Take any tabular dataset with >5% missingness. Fit a scaler on the full dataset, then fit it on train only. Compare test RMSE between the two pipelines.
  2. Deliberately create a temporal leak: shuffle a time-series dataset and split randomly. Watch validation performance look "too good."
  3. Fix it with a time-ordered split and an 11-day embargo. Quantify how much of the "performance" was leakage.

Chapter 4

Metrics

What you measure is what you get. A metric is a contract between the model and the business — pick the wrong one and the optimizer will find the most efficient way to fail your actual goal.

4.1 Classification, dissected

Every classification evaluation starts from the confusion matrix: TP true positives, FP false positives, TN true negatives, FN false negatives. From those four cells:

accuracy = (TP + TN) / N             # overall correctness — useless when classes are rare
precision =  TP / (TP + FP)          # of what you flagged, how much was real? (cost of false alarms)
recall     =  TP / (TP + FN)         # of what was real, how much did you catch? (cost of misses)
F1         =  2·P·R / (P + R)        # harmonic mean — punishes lopsidedness
Fβ         =  (1+β²)·P·R / (β²·P + R) # β>1 weights recall; β<1 weights precision

On an imbalanced dataset (fraud: 0.2% positive), a model that flags nothing scores 99.8% accuracy and catches nothing. Recall and precision are the honest currencies; F1 and Fβ let you encode the trade-off numerically — F2 says "missing cases hurt twice as much as false alarms."

ScenarioPriorityLead metric
Fraud / spam detectionDon't miss real fraud; false alarms tolerableRecall at fixed precision, PR-AUC
Medical screeningMissing disease is catastrophicSensitivity (recall) at high specificity
Ad click predictionFlags must be trustworthyPrecision, top-k lift
Balanced multiclassEven performance across classesMacro-averaged F1
Rare-class multiclassDon't let the majority drown the minorityWeighted F1 / per-class recall report

4.2 Ranking: ROC and PR curves

Real classifiers emit probabilities, and a threshold is a business decision — so evaluate the whole curve, not one cut point. ROC-AUC plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across all thresholds; it measures the probability that a random positive ranks above a random negative. Under extreme imbalance it looks flattering, because the FPR denominator is huge. PR-AUC plots precision against recall and is the correct lens when positives are rare — it answers "when I flag this many, how many are real?"

  • Use ROC-AUC when classes are reasonably balanced and you need a threshold-free summary. AUC = 0.5 is a coin; 0.9+ is strong; report the confidence interval, not just the point.
  • Use PR-AUC when positives are rare (under ~5%) or the cost asymmetry is extreme. A model can post great ROC-AUC and still be practically useless at the operating point you deploy at.

4.3 Regression metrics

MetricFormula / ideaBest for
MSEmean((y−ŷ)²)Default differentiable loss; punishes large errors hard
RMSE√MSEReporting in target units; same penalty profile as MSE
MAEmean(|y−ŷ|)Robustness to outliers; straight-line interpretation
HuberMSE near zero, MAE in the tailsNoisy labels — MSE's gradient with MAE's robustness
Quantile lossAsymmetric penalty per quantile τPrediction intervals, "95th percentile of delivery time"

Always pair a point metric with an error distribution: mean error (bias), a histogram of residuals, and a Q–Q plot. A model with zero mean error can still be systematically wrong in the tails, where the money is.

4.4 Language and generation metrics

  • Perplexity — exp(−log-likelihood); the model's effective branching factor. Excellent for tracking pretraining health; weak as a proxy for task quality.
  • BLEU / ROUGE — n-gram overlap with references. Fast and cheap, but they reward fluent generic text over correct specific text. Use for regression monitoring, not go/no-go decisions.
  • BERTScore — embedding similarity between generated and reference tokens. More tolerant of paraphrase; still reference-bound.
  • LLM-as-judge — a strong model grades outputs against a rubric. The current standard for open-ended quality, with real caveats: self-preference bias, positional bias, and rubric drift. Calibrate against human scores on a held-out set.
  • Task metrics — for grounded tasks (code, math, extraction), prefer execution pass rate, exact set match, or schema validation. Verifiable beats vibes.

4.5 Fairness and calibration

A global metric can hide a failing subgroup. Report your lead metric per slice — by demographic group, region, device, or traffic source — and set launch gates on the worst slice, not the mean. Complement this with calibration: if the model says 80%, do 80% of those cases actually occur? A reliability diagram (predicted probability vs. observed frequency) exposes overconfidence; temperature scaling and isotonic regression fix it post-hoc at near-zero cost.

4.6 Feeling the precision–recall trade-off

Imagine a fraud detector facing 900 true frauds among 99,100 legitimate transactions (0.9% positive rate). The table below sweeps the decision threshold over a synthetic score distribution and shows what "better" actually means when the classes are lopsided:

ThresholdRecallPrecisionCatches (TP)False alarms (FP)F1
0.3090.9%1.6%81849,5500.032
0.4082.1%2.4%73930,5720.046
0.5069.1%3.8%62215,7270.072
0.6053.3%6.8%4806,6200.120
0.7036.9%12.8%3322,2550.190
0.8022.7%24.9%2046150.237
0.9012.2%45.1%1101340.192
  • The left side (t ≤ 0.40) is maximum recall: you catch most fraud, but the false-alarm column is the story — at 0.30 you flag 49,550 clean transactions to stop 818 frauds.
  • The middle (0.50–0.70) is where operating decisions actually happen: recall falls from about 69% to 37%, while precision climbs from 4% to 13%.
  • The right side (t ≥ 0.80) buys trust at the price of coverage: at 0.90 a flagged case is real 45% of the time, yet you still miss 88% of fraud.

No single threshold wins; the right one is defined by your cost function — the price of a missed fraud versus the price of a wrongly flagged customer. (Numbers derive from synthetic score distributions — positives ≈ N(0.62, 0.24), negatives ≈ N(0.30, 0.20). The shape is the point, not the digits.)

Exercise 04
  1. On an imbalanced dataset, compute accuracy, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC for a model that always predicts the majority class. Note what each metric claims.
  2. Plot the precision-recall curve for your real model and find the threshold that maximizes F2.
  3. Report your lead metric on three slices you define (e.g., by sign-up channel). Which slice fails the launch gate?

Chapter 5

Training Methods

Optimization: walking a mountain range in the dark. The loss surface of a modern network is non-convex, wildly scaled, and studded with saddle points — training is the art of still finding a good valley.

5.1 Gradient descent and its descendants

Batch GD computes the exact gradient per step — accurate, but memory-heavy. SGD uses one sample — noisy, but the noise is a feature: it escapes sharp minima. Mini-batch SGD is the practical middle. Modern optimizers stack clever state on top of SGD:

OptimizerIdeaWhen to reach for it
MomentumAccumulates a velocity term; smooths oscillationsDefault upgrade over vanilla SGD for deep nets
AdaGradPer-parameter adaptive LR from accumulated gradientsSparse features (early NLP); LR decays too aggressively for dense nets
RMSPropExponentially-decayed adaptive LRFixes AdaGrad's decay; classic for RNNs
AdamMomentum + RMSProp (1st and 2nd moment estimates)The workhorse default; fast, forgiving hyperparameters
AdamWAdam with decoupled weight decayTransformers and large-scale training; the modern default
SGD + momentumThe classic, tuned carefullyOften edges out Adam on final accuracy for CV tasks if you have the tuning budget

5.2 Learning rate: the number that matters most

No hyperparameter changes outcomes as much as the learning rate. Too high and the loss diverges or oscillates forever; too low and you crawl. The modern playbook:

  • LR range test. Sweep log-spaced LRs for a few hundred steps; pick the highest rate whose loss is still descending — the "no-divergence point," often a hair below the minimum observed loss.
  • Warmup. Start small (1–5% of peak) and ramp linearly; stabilizes early training while normalization statistics are still settling.
  • Scheduled decay. Cosine annealing to a low floor is the transformer standard; step decay remains common in CV.
  • Batch-size coupling. Larger batches permit higher LRs (linear scaling rule), but reduce the beneficial noise — watch generalization.
  • Gradient clipping. Clip the global norm (typically to 1.0); cheap insurance against explosion, especially in RNNs and early transformer layers.

5.3 Regularization: the anti-overfit toolkit

TechniqueWhat it doesWhen to use it
AugmentationCrops, flips, color jitter, MixUp, cutmix; synonym dropout for text; controlled noise for tablesThe strongest regularizer in vision — if the validation gap is your problem, augment harder before touching the model
Weight decay and dropoutDecoupled L2 shrinks weights and smooths the landscape; dropout mutes units each step, forcing redundancyBoth cheap, both effective, both worth tuning — don't leave them at defaults forever
Early stopping and ensemblingStop when validation loss plateaus (free regularization with built-in model selection); ensemble seeds or architecturesEnsembling is the highest-leverage "last 2%" before you ship
Architectural and data-basedSmaller capacity, depthwise separable convs, distillation from a big teacher into a small studentAnd the quiet giant: more, better data beats most regularization tricks — spend there first

5.4 Diagnosing the two classic failures

Underfitting — the model is too weak

Train and validation loss are both high and still descending: the model hasn't learned the structure. Fixes: more capacity, better features, longer training, a higher learning rate. Check for bugs first — a loss that can't move is often a dead activation or a forgotten optimizer.step().

Overfitting — the model is memorizing

Train loss keeps falling while validation loss turns upward: the model is fitting noise. Fixes: more data, augmentation, dropout, weight decay, early stopping, a smaller model. If the gap is huge, suspect label noise or leakage before anything else.

5.5 Pretraining and fine-tuning

The modern training stack is layered. Pretraining learns general representations from massive unlabeled (or self-supervised) data — next-token prediction for text, masked modeling for encoders, denoising for diffusion. Fine-tuning adapts those weights to your task with far less data. Parameter-efficient variants — LoRA (low-rank adapters), prefix tuning, adapters — update a small fraction of the weights and make large-model adaptation practical on a single GPU. The rule of thumb: freeze the backbone, tune the head, add LoRA only when you need the capacity. And RLHF / DPO layers preference learning on top — for behavior, not just accuracy.

5.6 Scaling, hardware, and the practicalities of big training

  • Mixed precision (FP16 / BF16). Halves memory and roughly doubles throughput; BF16 is the safe default for large transformers, with loss scaling for FP16.
  • Gradient accumulation. Simulate a larger batch when the GPU can't hold one; mathematically equivalent (modulo batch-norm nuances).
  • Distributed strategies. Data parallelism (shard batches), tensor parallelism (shard layers), pipeline parallelism (shard stages), and ZeRO / FSDP (shard optimizer state and parameters). Choose by where your memory bottleneck is.
  • Checkpointing and fault tolerance. At scale, hardware will fail mid-run. Async checkpoints, elastic re-launch, and deterministic replay are part of the architecture, not an afterthought.
  • Scaling laws. Loss scales as a power law in model size, dataset size, and compute (Chinchilla: match tokens to parameters at roughly 20:1). Use them to decide the shape of your budget before you spend it.
  • Reproducibility. Pin seeds, log everything (W&B / MLflow), version data and code. A run you can't reproduce is a run you can't defend.
Exercise 05
  1. Run an LR range test on a small CNN. Plot loss vs. LR and identify the no-divergence point.
  2. Train the same net with and without warmup plus cosine decay. Measure final validation loss and the steps to reach 90% of the way there.
  3. Introduce deliberate overfitting (tiny batch, high LR, no decay). Then fix it one technique at a time and record which single change closed the train/validation gap the most.

Chapter 6

Beyond Training

A model isn't finished when it trains. It's finished when it's trusted. The final mile is where most projects actually die — not in the loss curve, but in the deployment, the drift, the stakeholder meeting, and the 2 a.m. incident.

6.1 Evaluation and model selection

Lock the test set. Run the full metric suite — lead metric, slices, calibration, latency, cost. Select the checkpoint by validation performance only, then report the test set once. If you look at the test set repeatedly, it becomes validation; that's why careful teams keep a "gold" set that is scored exactly twice, ever. Define the launch gates before the run, not after.

6.2 Optimization and packaging

Export to ONNX or a runtime format, quantize (INT8 / INT4) where accuracy holds, prune or distill if the serving budget is tight, and bake the preprocessing into the artifact. The model and its transforms ship as one unit — a model file without its scaler is a promise without a contract.

6.3 Serving and inference

Choose the topology: REST for simple requests, streaming for generation, batch for offline scoring. Batch aggressively — GPU utilization scales with batch size until latency dies. Set timeouts, rate limits, and a graceful fallback (cached answer, smaller model, human queue) for when the fast path fails.

6.4 Monitoring and drift

Track three families of signals: input drift (feature distributions vs. training), prediction drift (score distribution over time), and outcome drift (do labels still arrive, and does the model still predict them well?). Alert on PSI or KL divergence per feature; retraining triggers should be defined in advance, not invented in the incident channel.

6.5 Retraining and lifecycle

Schedule retraining on data freshness, not calendar convenience. Version every artifact — model, data, code, config — as a single deployable unit. Keep the last known-good checkpoint hot for instant rollback, and automate the champion/challenger comparison so a new model must beat the old one on the live eval set before it earns production.

6.6 Governance and continuous audit

Maintain the model card: intended use, known limitations, slice performance, and a named rollback owner. Run periodic fairness and safety audits, especially after any data or model change. Treat the model as a regulated surface — the same review rigor you'd give a payment system, scaled to its actual blast radius.

The MLOps loop, in one sentence

Capture → curate → train → evaluate → deploy → monitor → detect drift → re-capture. The loop, not the model, is the product.

Exercise 06
  1. Wrap your trained model in a FastAPI endpoint with a request validator and a 200 ms p95 budget. Load-test it and find where the bottleneck actually is.
  2. Compute PSI between your training features and the last 7 days of (simulated) production features. Which feature drifted most?
  3. Write the model card for your system in under 300 words. You will be amazed what you don't yet know about it.

Chapter 7

The Full Syllabus

Everything on one page. The complete course at a glance — use it as a checklist, a résumé line, or a hiring rubric.

7.1 Where to go from here

The canonical texts

Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville's Deep Learning is the mathematical spine; Caruana and colleagues' Practical Tips for Predicting Real-World Distributions collects the field's hard-won heuristics; Attention Is All You Need is the fifteen pages that reshaped the decade. Read the paper, then re-read it after building one.

The hands-on path

Rebuild each architecture from scratch in NumPy before using a framework. Then in PyTorch. Then at scale. The gaps between those three versions are where the real learning lives.

The career path

Ship one small model end-to-end — data, metric, deployment, monitoring — before chasing frontier research. Production scars teach what no paper can: what breaks, when, and why.

The last line of the course

The model is never finished; the work is. Data shifts, users adapt, and the metric that mattered in Q1 is stale by Q3. The practitioners who last aren't the ones who train the biggest model — they're the ones who run the loop honestly, measure what they claim, and ship what they can defend.

Glossary

Backpropagation
Application of the chain rule that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter in a single backward pass.
Batch size
The number of examples processed per optimizer step; interacts with learning rate, memory, and generalization.
Causal masking
The decoder-only trick of letting a position attend only to earlier positions, making next-token prediction well-defined.
Class imbalance
One label far rarer than the others, making accuracy misleading and precision/recall the honest metrics.
Data leakage
Information from validation/test (or the future) sneaking into training and inflating scores; the most common silent failure.
Drift
Live data distributions shifting away from training distributions, quietly degrading performance.
Embedding
A learned dense vector representation of a discrete item — a word, a user, an image patch.
Epoch
One full pass over the training data.
Fine-tuning
Adapting pretrained weights to a task with far less data.
Gradient
The direction of steepest ascent of the loss; optimizers step against it.
Inference
Running a trained model on new inputs — the latency and cost stage.
Overfitting
Fitting noise: training error falls while validation error rises.
Perplexity
exp(−average log-likelihood); a language model's effective branching factor.
Regularization
Any constraint that fights overfitting: weight decay, dropout, augmentation, early stopping, capacity limits.
Residual connection
A skip link, y = F(x) + x, that lets gradients flow through deep networks.
Warmup
The short opening phase of training in which the learning rate ramps up from a small value.

Further Study

Books

  • Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, Aaron Courville — Deep Learning. The mathematical spine of the field.
  • Aurélien Géron — Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow. Practical momentum for every chapter of this book.
  • Caruana, Niculescu-Miziel, Crew, Kirsch — Practical Tips for Predicting Real-World Distributions. Working paper, but the field's best collection of heuristics.

Papers

  • Vaswani et al. (2017) — Attention Is All You Need. The transformer, in fifteen pages.
  • Devlin et al. (2018) — BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers. Encoder-side pretraining.
  • Hu et al. (2021) — LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
  • Hoffmann et al. (2022) — Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models. Scaling laws (Chinchilla).

Practice

  • Rebuild each architecture in this book in three fidelities: NumPy, PyTorch, at scale. The gaps between the versions are the course.
  • Ship one model end-to-end — data, metric, deployment, monitoring — before reading the next paper.

| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Tome.html`     | The complete ebook in one book-styled file. Open it in any browser.   |
| `make_epub.sh`  | **Primary** EPUB builder — one command, powered by Pandoc             |
| `make_epub.py`  | **Fallback** EPUB builder — Python 3 stdlib only, no Pandoc needed    |
| `README.md`     | This guide — how to build EPUB and MOBI                               |

The ebook mirrors the webpage course: 7 chapters (Foundations, Architectures,
Data, Metrics, Training, Beyond Training, Practice) plus preface, glossary,
further-study, and colophon — with a clickable table of contents.

> **Use `make_epub.sh` (Pandoc) unless you have a reason not to.**
> Pandoc emits a clean, standards-compliant EPUB 3 that opens reliably in
> strict readers (Foliate, Apple Books, Kobo, Calibre). The Python script is
> kept as a dependency-free fallback for machines without Pandoc.

---

## 1) Build the EPUB — primary method: Pandoc

Requires **Pandoc** (plus `sed`, which is preinstalled on Linux/macOS):

```bash
sudo apt install pandoc        # Debian / Ubuntu
# brew install pandoc          # macOS
# winget install pandoc        # Windows
```

Then, from this folder:

```bash
./make_epub.sh                 # → builds Tome.epub
```

The script does four things:

1. extracts the book's `<style>` block from `Tome.html` into a temp CSS file,
2. appends a few reader overrides (white background, per-chapter page breaks),
3. runs `pandoc` with explicit metadata, `--toc`, and the stylesheet flag
   appropriate for your Pandoc version (see below),
4. cleans up the temp file and prints the result.

**Stylesheet flag differs by Pandoc version.** Pandoc 3.x renamed the flag
to `--css` and *removed* the old one (it hard-fails on unknown flags, so the
wrong name aborts the build); Pandoc 2.x only knows `--epub-stylesheet`.
`make_epub.sh` auto-detects which your installation accepts (it checks the
`--help` output). If you run Pandoc by hand:

```bash
# Pandoc 3.x:
pandoc Tome.html -o Tome.epub --toc --css=/tmp/book.css
# Pandoc 2.x:
pandoc Tome.html -o Tome.epub --toc --epub-stylesheet=/tmp/book.css
```

Full manual recipe, if you prefer to run it by hand:

```bash
sed -n '/<style[^>]*>/,/<\/style>/p' Tome.html | sed '1d;$d' > /tmp/book.css \
  && echo 'html,body{background:#fff}.chapter{page-break-before:always}' >> /tmp/book.css \
  && pandoc Tome.html -o Tome.epub --toc --split-level=1 --css=/tmp/book.css \
     --metadata title="Curriculum: A Field Course in Creating AI Models" \
     --metadata author="Field Course Press" --metadata language=en --metadata date=2025
```

Notes specific to `Tome.html`:

- **Metadata is stated explicitly.** From HTML input Pandoc only harvests the
  `<title>` — it ignores the `author` and `description` meta tags, hence the
  `--metadata` flags.
- **`--toc`** auto-builds a clickable table of contents from the chapter and
  section headings — no hand-crafted nav needed.
- **`--split-level=1`** keeps each chapter as its own file in the EPUB
  (Pandoc's default of 2 would split at every section, which strands each
  chapter title at the bottom of the previous section's page).
- The stylesheet flag (`--css` / `--epub-stylesheet`) bundles the book's
  typography (callouts, code boxes, tables, exercises). Omit it and you get
  Pandoc's plain default look.
- Code blocks lose their per-token coloring (the `<span>` markup inside
  `<pre>` is flattened to plain text); everything else converts cleanly.

Validate the result (optional):

- **Calibre**: *Tools → Check book* → select `Tome.epub`.
- **Online**: <https://validate.idpf.org> (W3C EPUB validator).
- **Quick test**: open it in Foliate, Apple Books, Kobo, or the free
  [Calibre E-book Viewer](https://calibre-ebook.com).

### Fallback: Python (no Pandoc)

If you have no Pandoc but have **Python 3.8+** (standard library only — no
pip packages):

```bash
python3 make_epub.py                  # builds Tome.epub next to the script
python3 make_epub.py --out MyBook.epub
```

It splits the HTML at its `<!-- PART:... -->` markers into one XHTML file per
chapter, writes an EPUB 3 package with a hand-crafted `nav` **and** legacy
NCX, and validates every generated XML document before writing the zip.
Expected differences from the Pandoc output: one chapter per file (nicer for
some readers), per-token code coloring preserved, and a hand-built TOC.

## 2) Convert EPUB → MOBI (Kindle)

> Note: Amazon has been migrating Kindle to **KFX** and continues to accept
> **EPUB** directly in many places (including Kindle Personal Document email
> and "Send to Kindle"), so EPUB is often the safest upload. MOBI is still
> supported by the Calibre/Kindle pipeline below. **Pandoc cannot write
> MOBI** — Calibre is the step that produces it, from either EPUB.

**Option A — Calibre (recommended, free, cross-platform)**

1. Install [Calibre](https://calibre-ebook.com).
2. Double-click `Tome.epub` to add it to the library (or *Add books*).
3. Select it → **Convert books** (or press `K`).
4. In the *Output format* dropdown, choose **MOBI** (or **AZW3** for newer
   Kindles, which renders the layout better).
5. (Optional) Metadata tab: set title, author, language.
6. *OK* → find `Tome.mobi` in your Calibre library folder.

**Option B — Calibre Command Line (calibre-ebook-convert)**

```bash
# after installing Calibre (its CLI is on PATH on most systems):
calibre-ebook-convert Tome.epub Tome.mobi
# or, for better rendering on modern Kindles:
calibre-ebook-convert Tome.epub Tome.azw3
```

Useful flags:

```bash
calibre-ebook-convert Tome.epub Tome.mobi \
  --title "Curriculum: A Field Course in Creating AI Models" \
  --author "Field Course Press" \
  --language en
```

**Option C — Send to Kindle (no MOBI at all)**

Email the `.epub` to your registered `name@kindle.com` address (from a
whitelisted sender), or drag it onto the *Send to Kindle* web app.

## 3) Other formats (Calibre converts all of these)

```bash
calibre-ebook-convert Tome.epub Tome.pdf      # print-friendly
calibre-ebook-convert Tome.epub book.fb2      # FB2
calibre-ebook-convert Tome.epub book.kepub    # Kobo
```

Or use the GUI: select the book → *Convert books* → pick any output format.

## 4) Read it right now

`Tome.html` opens directly in any browser — no build step, no network needed
(it uses system serif and monospace fonts). The Contents page links jump to
each chapter in the browser, and become the reader's clickable table of
contents once converted to EPUB. Print it too: the file carries dedicated
print styles with per-chapter page breaks.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom                              | Fix                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pandoc: command not found`          | `sudo apt install pandoc` (see section 1)                             |
| `--epub-stylesheet has been removed. Use --css instead.` | You have Pandoc 3.x; the old flag no longer exists. `make_epub.sh` auto-detects this — re-run it. (Hand-run: use `--css=/path/file.css`.) |
| `sed` missing (rare, e.g. minimal containers) | Use the Python fallback: `python3 make_epub.py`               |
| EPUB looks plain, no callouts/code styling | The stylesheet wasn't attached — re-run `./make_epub.sh` (it handles this) or add `--epub-stylesheet` |
| TOC not clickable in a very old reader | Re-convert through Calibre (it rewrites metadata and TOC)            |
| MOBI looks cramped                   | Prefer AZW3 instead of MOBI                                          |
| Foliate: `Cannot destructure property 'parentNode'` (or similar) | Your EPUB came from the old Python build. Rebuild with the primary Pandoc route: `./make_epub.sh` |
| `python3` not found (for the fallback) | Install Python 3 from <https://python.org>, or use `py make_epub.py` on Windows |
| Changed the text, want a new build   | Just re-run `./make_epub.sh` (or the Python script) — it reads `Tome.html` fresh each time |

files.make_epub.sh:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# make_epub.sh — PRIMARY method: build Tome.epub from Tome.html with Pandoc.
#
# Pandoc emits a clean, standards-compliant EPUB 3 that opens reliably in
# strict readers (Foliate, Apple Books, Kobo, Calibre). This is the
# recommended route. (make_epub.py remains as a Python-only fallback.)
#
# Requires : pandoc, sed, bash        (sudo apt install pandoc)
# Produces : Tome.epub next to this script
#
set -euo pipefail

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
SRC="$HERE/Tome.html"
OUT="$HERE/Tome.epub"
CSS="$(mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/book.XXXXXX.css")"
trap 'rm -f "$CSS"' EXIT

command -v pandoc >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
  echo "error: pandoc not found — install it with:  sudo apt install pandoc" >&2
  exit 1
}
[ -f "$SRC" ] || { echo "error: source not found: $SRC" >&2; exit 1; }

# 1. Pull the book's single <style> block out of the <head>
#    (the block lives inside the <head>, so this does not catch the
#     print/@media CSS that appears later in the file).
sed -n '/<style[^>]*>/,/<\/style>/p' "$SRC" | sed '1d;$d' > "$CSS"

# 2. Append reader-friendly overrides at the END so they win the cascade
#    (white background + per-chapter page breaks in paginated readers).
cat >> "$CSS" <<'CSSEOF'

/* -- EPUB reader overrides (appended by make_epub.sh) -- */
html{background:#fff}
body{background:#fff}
.part{max-width:none;padding:2.2em 0.4em 3em}
.part+.part{border-top:0}
.chapter{page-break-before:always}
.cover{text-align:center;padding-top:16vh}
CSSEOF

# 3. Convert. Metadata is stated explicitly (Pandoc ignores <head> meta tags
#    for EPUB), --toc builds a clickable table of contents, and the stylesheet
#    flag bundles the book's typography. Newer Pandoc renamed
#    --epub-stylesheet to --css (and removed the old flag), so pick whichever
#    this installation knows.
if pandoc --help 2>/dev/null | grep -q -- --epub-stylesheet; then
  # older Pandoc (2.x): EPUB-specific stylesheet flag
  CSS_OPT=(--epub-stylesheet)
else
  # newer Pandoc (3.x): --epub-stylesheet was removed; --css is the successor
  CSS_OPT=(--css)
fi
echo "Using stylesheet flag: ${CSS_OPT[0]} (pandoc $(pandoc --version | head -n1 | grep -oE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?'))"

pandoc "$SRC" -o "$OUT" \
  --toc \
  --split-level=1 \
  "${CSS_OPT[@]}"="$CSS" \
  --metadata title="Curriculum: A Field Course in Creating AI Models" \
  --metadata author="Field Course Press" \
  --metadata language=en \
  --metadata date=2025

echo "Built $OUT with Pandoc."
echo "Open it in Foliate / Apple Books / Kobo. For MOBI/AZW3, see README.md (section 3)."
